speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Yesterday during the time allotted for statements pursuant to Standing Order 21 the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) made a very useful intervention with respect to the situation in Manitoba. There was some commotion in the House at the time. I should explain to the House, and I want it to go on the record, that Your Honour's remarks at that time were very helpful.
At the time that my hon. friend was making his statement pursuant to Standing Order 21 I do not think there was a realization on this side of the House that Premier Pawley had resigned as Leader of the Party. Naturally, we understood that the Government of Manitoba had been defeated but there was no understanding that he had resigned as Leader of the Party.
My friend from Churchill made reference to the contribution that Premier Pawley had made to his province and to Canada. We also recognize that, although we may not agree on philosophies.
I want to have it made clear on the record that the natural partisan nature of the House spilled over at that point. But at the time I do not think there was a realization that the Premier of Manitoba had resigned as Leader of the Party.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour and the privilege of tabling petitions signed by residents of Saint-Leonard, Montreal North, Aylmer, Hull and Pointe-Claire, all in Quebec.
Your petitioners believe that by signing the Free Trade Agreement, the Mulroney Government sold out Canada without getting anything in return, and that Canadian industries still have no protection against U.S. trade laws. They also believe that the jobs of thousands of Canadians, especially women, are threatened, and that the Conservative Government has yet to make any provision for helping them through the transition period.
Therefore, your petitioners humbly pray Parliament to condemn the Government for having signed the Mulroney-Reagan Agreement.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also welcome this opportunity to table a petition signed by a number of constituents in my riding and neighbouring ridings. The undersigned refuse to eat irradiated food and are opposed to the construction of food irradiation centres. They ask for the immediate withdrawal of all irradiated food now on the market that does not bear the international symbol for irradiated products, and that such withdrawal be legislated.
They also ask that all irradiated products be labelled as follows: "This product has been irradiated with radioactive isotopes as a preservative measure; the effects on health are unknown".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 106 it is my honour to present a petition on behalf of a number of constituents who believe that the federal Government lacks a mandate from the people of Canada to conclude a trade deal with the United States.
The petitioners believe that the trade deal that was negotiated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) threatens the fabric of Canadian political and economic sovereignty since it removes the power of the Canadian Government to control foreign ownership in Canada, and it removes the ability of the Canadian Government to develop Canadian energy resources in the best interests of Canadians. It also eliminates or severely reduces the possibility of equalizing opportunities between the regions of Canada.
The petitioners believe that this trade deal would deny Canada the policy freedom to determine its own economic future, and thereby undermine our ability as Canadians to develop a society distinct from that of the United States.
The petitioners call upon Parliament to dissolve in order to allow the people of Canada an opportunity to decide on this trade deal during a national general election.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SIKH ORGANIZATIONS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Secretary of State for External Affairs erred seriously in urging upon the Provincial Premiers a political boycott of three Sikh organizations in Canada, thereby condemning entire groups on the basis of unsubstantiated allegations against individuals and, consequently undermining the multicultural fabric of Canadian society;
That this House, while condemning violence and terrorism as political instruments, affirms that all Canadian citizens, regardless of origin must not be subjected to any coercion, intimidation or other action by the Government designed to prevent their free and peaceful expression of their opinions and concerns about events and issues in Canada or in other lands; and
That this House therefore demands that the Government provide Parliament with all relevant information that led to its aforementioned communication with the Provinces and provide the Canadian Sikh community with a full, public opportunity to defend its honour and integrity and that the Government immediately withdraw its allegations and issue a full apology to all Canadians, and to the Canadian Sikh community in particular, for initiating an unprovoked attack on the rights and freedoms of Canadian citizens and for thereby subverting federal multiculturalism policy.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is with a certain degree of sadness that I raise on behalf of my Liberal caucus colleagues the matter before the House of Commons, and it is with a great deal of sadness that I have had to rise in my place over the last number of days to ask the Government, particularly the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), to account for the letter he wrote and sent to seven Premiers which urged a boycott of the activities of Sikh organizations.
I believe that those actions constitute an undermining of the social and cultural fabric which is Canada as we know it. They dangerously play with that very tender fabric by attacking the

March 10, 1988
Supply
dignity and honour of an entire membership of Canadians in three organizations. In this attack I believe that the Government is contributing to, perhaps not intentionally, but the fallout is contributing to and aggravating racial tensions and race relations in Canada.
While it is with sadness that I rise in my place, I believe it is a necessary undertaking, because we must constantly remind ourselves as a Parliament that our country is as strong as its treatment of its weakest minorities within its borders.
We know that the Canadian Sikh community has been besieged in recent days and in recent times. However, this should not condone its further abuse as a member of the Canadian community or as a member of the Canadian family.
I am confused and bewildered by the letter from the Secretary of State for External Affairs, because only last June, 1987, at a convention of the World Sikh Organization in Vancouver, the following message was brought to the membership:
-I am delighted to extend my warmest greetings and sincere best wishes to the members of the World Sikh Organization of Canada.
The Sikh community in Canada represents an important component of this country's multicultural structure, one which we, as Canadians, are proud of. Ours is a nation that has been strengthened by the cultural and ethnic diversity of its peoples; by celebrating your role in Canadian society you are helping to unite not only the people of your community, but the people of Canada as well.
On behalf of the Government of Canada, may I wish the members of your community continued health and prosperity.
That letter was signed by no less than the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and sent to the same organization in June, 1987. It is the same organization which is now being targeted for political boycott.
In 1985, a year after the Government took office, at another conference of the same organization a message was delivered by the Hon. Member for Cariboo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway) of the Conservative Party, in which he said:
-I am here today not representing the Government of Canada, but 1 am here as an independent individual Member of Parliament. 1 do however have the blessings of the Minister of External Affairs, the Right Hon. Joe Clark.
Therefore I am confused, as a Member of Parliament, that only last June the Prime Minister of Canada publicly congratulated, welcomed, and recognized this organization, and then in the same year, while one thing was being done publicly, the exact opposite was being advocated secretly. I bring that to the attention of the House of Commons because I believe to a certain degree that those two contradictory actions are deplorable.
First, there are two problems with the letter-one is procedural and one is on substance. From a procedural viewpoint, I question why the Secretary of State for External Affairs only sent the letter to seven Premiers, not to all of them. Why were federal Members of Parliament not sent the letter if it was a matter of urgent necessity? Why were the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) and the Leader of the New Democratic Party, the Hon. Member for
Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), not briefed and provided with the same information? Why were municipal leaders not advised?
I am talking about the elected leadership of the country who work and mingle with the community organizations from which the Secretary of State for External Affairs asked the Premiers to dissociate themselves. On top of that, we only found out about the existence of the letter through a leak. If it were not leaked, we would not be having the debate today; we would still be in the dark.
Therefore, this leads me to ask what other letters have been written and sent to various elected representatives in the country about the Sikh organizations or the Sikh communities? What other ethnocultural groups have been targeted with similar letters?
Finally, on the question of procedure, I find it puzzling that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has asked us to be ignorant and to ignore these three organizations. If we take a very different example-and I admit that it is a very different example-in South Africa, the Minister said that notwithstanding the fact that we believe that the Botha Government in South Africa is a repugnant, offensive regime which continues to prop up institutionalized racism, as bad and as evil as we know that Government to be, we will not break diplomatic relations because we will try to have that flicker of hope remain so that we can change a bad situation into a good one from within.
To a certain degree I sympathize, although we have taken a somewhat different attitude, with the attempted logic and sincerity of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. However, if we accept that attitude with that evil regime and, to a lesser degree, if the Minister has proof of individual members of these organizations having clearly participated, with evidence, in various violent activities, why would he not try to keep the channels of communication open with these organizations to bring these people to justice and to try to work from within rather than to say to the Premiers to treat individual organizations and the Canadian members of these organizations as political lepers?
How will ignorance produce justice? How are we to stem the tide if these elements exist in any organization or community, if we in fact send out a letter saying, "Don't bother with these organizations"? It does not solve the problem.
As I have mentioned, the second problem is the question of substance. One justification for the letter is that the Minister stated that there were some members who were engaged in these activities. In the letter to the Premiers he said:
Some members of these organizations have also engaged in or promote
violent activities-
Is that proper justification for the letter? Why take an unproven or alleged matter, a matter of individual responsibility, and transpose it into a blanket of collective guilt which covers all Canadian membership in those organizations? Why
March 10, 1988

be a contributor to creating a stigma which is difficult for that community to shake?
This is not a problem faced by only first generation Canadians of that community. It is a stigma which takes root in their youngsters, in the young men and women who should have the same future and opportunities in the country, but because of the stigma they start at a different place than do their peers in Canadian society.
Why does the federal Government, through this letter, begin to equate Sikhism with terrorism by that collective guilt allegation? There have been enough injustices in the past that one would have thought we would have avoided another occurrence, that we would have avoided bringing further pain and in some quarters, further shame in being who you are in this country.
We had the situation of the Japanese Canadian redress where Canadian citizens were discriminated blatantly by governments and other Canadians because of who they were. We still have elements in our society that lay the blame on the whole dark episode of Naziism on the doorsteps of certain German Canadian elements in this country. Recently in my own community, in the Canadian Italian community, certain elements have tried to equate Italianism with the Mafia. That hurts, Mr. Speaker. First it hurts because it is not true of that community. Second, it hurts because it creates baggage which must be carried, not by one generation but by second and third generation Canadians.
While every sensible Canadian condemns terrorism and any act of violence as a means of arriving at any end, which is shared by all Members and Parties in this House, it does not give the Government or the Minister the right or the licence to take on an individual responsibility and say, "Therefore, the collectivity of that membership is guilty". That is not the way our justice system works in Canada.
If there are cases of individual responsibilities, then what is achieved by this letter? Does this letter bring those individual members to justice? Does this letter provide us with the evidence that would suggest that certain members perhaps should face justice? What gain do we have by painting those three organizations and, through other debates, the community with that same brush?
The Secretary of State for External Affairs who will participate in this debate may say that certain members within the world Sikh organizations at some time or other may have said certain things. He might draw to the attention of the House that a certain Secretary General of the World Sikh Organization, General Bhullar Singh, may have said at one point that he would like to obtain arms to help obtain a homeland. Mr. Didar Bains, the United States Vice-President of the World Sikh Organization may have made statements suggesting that the assassination of Mrs. Ghandi was a legitimate means to achieve that end.
Supply
There was a debate whether or not those statements were said. Assuming they were said, this Member, this Party, dissociate ourselves with those statements. More important, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian membership in these organizations, attacked by the Minister, who are in this Chamber participating and listening to this debate, have dissociated themselves from those comments, if they were ever made, and condemn those comments, if they were ever made. Those statements were deposited with me in my own office when I raised these issues. Therefore, I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs, if he has the Canadian membership of these organizations which dissociate themselves from these statements, why prosecute, through this letter, the collectivity?
The second justification for the letter is to propose a boycott because these groups advocated an independent Sikh homeland in India. The Minister writes to the Premiers:
I would appreciate your co-operation in avoiding events and activities which
could be perceived as supporting the Sikh organizations mentioned above or
their objective in the creation of an independent Sikh state.
This issue of an independent homeland is clearly a foreign issue which is sovereign only to the citizens of India who in the end, in their own time, in their own way, must come to grips with that. Since when should our federal Government take sides on an issue, state its preference in favour of the current Indian administration and then on its strength punish Canadians of Sikh origin in Canada who may not share this view? How could the rights of full citizenship in this country with the freedom of participating in the community and political life of Canada be denied and infringed upon by a government which urges a boycott of those organizations?
Foreign policy is an outgrowth of domestic policy. Foreign policy is a reflection of the principles, the ideals and the aspirations to which we as a Canadian people subscribe. We cannot always do and say what the world wants us to do and say. Instead, we must do and we must say what the Canadian citizens permit us as a society to say. Therefore, the Secretary of State for External Affairs has the standards for a foreign policy backwards. He should not be putting it backwards because there are serious repercussions with that procedure.
What happens if the Government of Yugoslavia were to call or write our Minister and say, "We don't want your politicians associating themselves with Croatian Canadian clubs". If Greece were to do the same thing with Turkish Canadian clubs, what then? What about the situation between the Sinhalese and the Tamils? We cannot be coerced or intimidated into taking a certain foreign stand on an issue and allowing that issue to undermine rights of Canadians back home, whoever those Canadians are, wherever they came from and however long they have been in this country.
The Minister for External Affairs is either the Minister for External Affairs for Canada or he is the Minister of External Affairs for India. If he is the Minister of External Affairs for the latter, he might have some justification for saying the things he did because that would be his prerogative. But he is

March 10, 1988
Supply
not the Minister of External Affairs for India. He is a Canadian Minister, a Canadian Member of Parliament, who must always maintain the first rule, which is to stand up for Canada and stand up for Canadians whoever those Canadians may be. He abdicated that responsibility and I draw it to this attention.
The third and final justification for the Minister's letter is that the boycott was favoured to a certain degree by the Government of India. Again, the Minister writes in his letter:
The activities of these organizations have been a significant irritant in our relations with India. The Government of India has taken particular exception when elected officials attend functions sponsored by these organizations.
The Minister is implying that the reason he wrote the letter was to secure relations with India. Past governments have always tried to secure a working respectable relationship with India. Previous Liberal administrations did not do so to the detriment of Canadians back home. We were not willing, in order to enjoy the favour of the existing Indian Government, to sacrifice Canadians of Sikh origin here, nor should we in any relationship with any other government. But this Government was prepared to sacrifice the citizenship of Canadians back home. One would have at least expected the Indian authorities to have defended, come forward and supported the Minister. But what happened, Mr. Speaker? Well, I will tell you what happened. A spokesperson for the Indian High Commission in Ottawa completely dissociated herself from that letter. She was quoted as saying in a Globe and Mail article for February 26:
But India has not complained about the involvement of elected officials with these groups, she said.
"What transpires between federal and provincial governments in Canada is purely an internal matter".
Those were the words of Mrs. Tripathi of the Indian High Commission. I asked the Minister the other day whether he could explain the discrepancy. Could he explain why the Indian High Commission in Ottawa is saying that it did not order or suggest a political boycott? I asked why the Minister implied in his letter to the Premiers that that was the case. If it did not come from the Indian Government, then what was the justification and by whom was that seed planted? That brings us to the issue that is at the heart of this dilemma.
This is more than a struggle for the Canadian Sikh community. Naturally, they feel the most pain and they feel the challenge of overcoming the stigma of yet another attack. However, this struggle has manifested itself in other communities. This latest allegation, an official statement of the Conservative Government, tramples also on the larger question of the principles underpinning our multiculturalism policy and the multiculturalism that is the reality of Canada.
It is sad to see that the Minister of State for multiculturalism has been silent during this entire debate. It is equally deplorable that the Secretary of State for External Affairs, rather than coming forward with evidence that would in any
way substantiate the actions his letter recommends, rather than retract his letter in the absence of such evidence, prefers to hide behind these general, unproven allegations that cut Canadians deeply.
I see that you are indicating that my time is just about up, Mr. Speaker. I appeal to the Chair for some understanding because of the sensitivity of this issue. I conclude by saying that the Government has the responsibility to provide the House and, and through it, Canadians with an inquiry so that we may have the documentation and information that is in the possession of the Government of Canada that prompted such action. This inquiry would provide a forum in which Canadians, members of these three organizations and members of the larger Canadian Sikh community could defend their honour, their integrity and their place within Canada. If there is to be no such inquiry, then the Minister ought to withdraw the letter or apologize for writing it.
The Premier of B.C. has refused to respect the Minister's letter. The Premier of Ontario does not support the letter, despite claims made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in the House. Members of provincial legislatures across Canada are writing to say that they will not follow the letter. Members of the Government's own Conservative Party have publicly criticized and attacked the Minister's letter. The Minister should finally realize, therefore, that he is becoming increasingly isolated in his defence of the indefensible.
I ask the Minister today to do the honourable thing, to provide this House with the evidence so that we can get to the issue at hand and clear the name of this community.
Finally, we in this House must recognize one unmistakable, unquestionable reality. History has placed all of us in Canada within one common border and under one common law. All of us, from the most powerful and the wealthiest of men to the poorest of children share one possession; that is, being Canadian. Granted, it is difficult to know from time to time what that precisely means because it means so many different things to so many different people. In part, to be a Canadian means to have once been a stranger, to have left the old and familiar for the new. But it also means that those who deny the strangers among us also deny the strength and the future of Canada. I ask the Government to stop denying Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to my hon. friend's comments. I must say that 1 agree, by and large, with the points he was raising.
The Hon. Member knows, of course, of the wounded feeling which exists within the Sikh community across Canada today as a result of recent developments. However, that is part of an ongoing process, and the Hon. Member will be well aware of that.
While I listened to the Hon. Member's remarks I could not help but think that years ago Jews living in Canada urged and worked toward the creation of the State of Israel. Today, Palestinians as well as Canadian citizens are urging the creation of a homeland for Palestinians. On Parliament Hill we have seen demonstrations of people of Croatian origin urging the creation of a Croatian state. We have seen Ukrainians, Slovaks and a long list of people appear on Parliament Hill, all in their own way, and I might add in their own peaceful way with an emphasis on the word "peaceful", indicating their concern for the creation of a homeland or a state for their people.
Is there something different here? Again, people of the Sikh faith are urging the creation of a homeland for their people. I do not see much difference between that and the Jews some years back urging the creation of the State of Israel.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SIKH ORGANIZATIONS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member poses a very interesting question. He asked about the similarity between the struggle for a defensible State of Israel and the one that is being advocated by Sikhs in India through peaceful means. Those human struggles are the same. Although there are different forces at play in those different regions of the world, the human desire to live in peace and in dignity and to have a place to stand is shared, whether we are talking about an independent homeland for Sikhs in India or about the struggle of Jews who wanted to be able to live behind identifiable and defensible borders.
The second aspect of this question is the more delicate part. When previous Governments of Canada supported clearly and unequivocally a state for Israel, those Governments did not create a backlash affecting Canadians of Arab or Palestinian descent. Regardless of our position on Israel, that position was not used as a way of politically boycotting the Arab community. We did not suggest to the premiers that they treat those individuals as political lepers because we supported a state for Israel.
What we have here is a double standard. As far as we know, we did not politically boycott those Palestinian and Arab elements within Canada at that time. Those people are now Canadians because being an immigrant must stop at a certain point in one's life. The word "immigration" describes a process. However, after you have been here 5 years, 10 years
Supply
or 20 years and you take the oath, you are a Canadian and the immigration process is behind you.
What is happening here is that the Secretary of State for External Affairs is saying that he agrees with India not granting an independent homeland for Sikhs. That is debatable given the fact of the state of Israel. Yet more importantly, the fact that the three organizations mentioned in the December 11 letter stand for an independent Sikh homeland in India is used as justification for boycotting those organizations. That is the shame. That is the knife wound.
Canadians, regardless of background, have freedom of speech. They are free to meet and discuss local issues or issues from afar in a non-violent, non-subversive way. I find it offensive that a foreign policy initiative is undermining domestic policy with respect to the rights of Canadians. We cannot allow that. Domestic policy draws its strength from a secure situation at home. It is only from that secure base that we can export our freedom, our democracy, our progressive vision to help an ailing world.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SIKH ORGANIZATIONS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to begin with, I might caution Hon. Members of the House about drawing parallels between the situation in India respecting Khalistan and other events in the world. I think before they begin to make those statements in the name of their Party, which there is some temptation to do by both my friend from Kamloops-Shuswap and the Hon. Member who introduced the motion, they would want to carefully consider the implications of what they are saying.
Sir, I intend to be as dispassionate as I can be in this debate. I think it would be helpful if I began by reading the letter in which the Official Opposition wants to make an issue. The letter was tabled in the House the other day and it states:
I am writing to you concerning possible invitations to you or members of your government to attend functions organized by members of the Canadian Sikh community.
The majority of these invitations are valuable in ensuring that your Government is kept informed of developments in the Sikh community and that the community is encouraged to participate fully in Canadian life.
There are, however, three Sikh organizations which exist largely to advocate the creation of an independent Sikh state, known as "Khalistan". These three organizations are the Babbar Khalsa, the International Sikh Youth Federation, and the World Sikh Organization. Some members of these organizations have also engaged in or promote violent activities aimed at Indian interests in Canada and elsewhere. The activities of these organizations have been a significant irritant in our relations with India. The Government of India has taken particular exception when elected officials attend functions sponsored by these organizations.
I fully understand the dilemma that elected officials face in making decisions as to which functions to attend. In some instances the sponsoring organization may not be readily apparent. Despite these difficulties, I would appreciate your co-operation in avoiding events and activities which could be perceived as supporting the Sikh organizations mentioned above or their objective in the creation of an independent Sikh state.
I would also request that you consider circulating a copy of this letter to members of your Cabinet and caucus. Should you require any additional information on this matter, please contact me.
That was the content of the letter which the Liberal Party is seeking to generate a debate over. I had hoped this sensitive issue would not be exploited for partisan purposes but the Liberal Party has chosen to put a motion forward in this House and therefore we will reply.
Sir, no one in this House should need reminding that modern societies are complex, and they are becoming more complex. Unhappily, one element of that complexity, one phase of modern international and national life, is that there is an increasing recourse to violence, not simply in the world
apart from Canada but also in Canada. All civilized societies wish to work to overcome those tendencies toward violence, to deal with the root causes, to not participate innocently in the encouraging of activities which might have a violent consequence. Certainly that is a deep commitment of this country and this Government.
Sir, we must not forget that Canadians have been victims of terrorism both at home and abroad. The pervasive fear that affected all Canadians as a result of the terrorism of the October crisis in Canada in 1970 can never be far from our minds. Even more recently Canadians have experienced the tragic consequences of terrorism. Canadians narrowly escaped death in the hijacking at Karachi in 1986. Canadians were aboard the Italian cruise ship, the Achille Lauro, which was hijacked in September, 1985, which was the scene of the murder of one of the passengers by terrorists. Three hundred and twenty-nine people, most of them Canadians, died in the Air India tragedy in 1985. A Canadian was killed in the attack on the Turkish Embassy in 1985 and in the same year Toronto's subway system was held hostage by terrorists. In November of that year a Canadian mother and her infant son lost their lives in a terrorist attack on an Egyptian airliner in Malta. In 1986 there was an assassination attempt against a visiting Indian state cabinet Minister on Vancouver Island.
In the course of my responsibilities I have stood at the graveside in Beiseker, Alberta, when the Canadian woman and her infant son, victims of terrorism abroad, were laid to rest in Canada. In the carrying out of my functions I have been representing Canada and this Parliament on the peninsula near Cork in Ireland where a memorial is established to the Canadian victims of the Air India tragedy. Sir, I have been to too many funerals to take this question lightly. Yet I am acutely aware that other of my colleagues in other countries less orderly and less free than ours have been to more funerals.
We have an obligation in this House to the nature, the freedom, and the multicultural reality of Canada, to ensure that we do everything that we can to allow Canadians to pursue their goals and live their lives in peace and freedom.
As I said in the House on the occasion of the death of Valinda Leonard and her infant son in the Egyptian air incident, no nation is immune to the scourge of terrorism. It is for this reason that it is essential that we pursue with our allies the development of concrete measures to combat terrorism. Similarly, we must put in place protective measures at home and be vigilant in ensuring the prevention of occasions and opportunities for terrorism to incubate or to strike.
That, Sir, if I may say so, is particularly important in a country like Canada precisely because we are a multicultural nation that encourages people to come here from every corner and every colour of the world and to follow their goals, their religions, and their views here in Canada in accordance with Canadian law. There is more opportunity for more people to
March 10, 1988

come here to express their traditions, to live their lives, than is the case in many other countries. As we provide more opportunity, that imposes upon us a greater obligation of care and imposes upon public officials a greater sense of responsibility.
The obligation is greater for us also because we are a free nation and we take our freedom seriously. It is protected in the courts, it is enshrined in the Charter, it is part of the practice of life in Canada. Sir, we all know the elemental reality that there can be no freedom for a society if there are not restraints accepted by individuals. Some of those restraints are set out in law and in policy.
Surely, Sir, we who hold the trust as public office holders have a particular obligation to ensure that laws are respected in Canada, to ensure that this country and its officials do not inadvertently become instruments of organizations or of interests which might seek the dismemberment of friendly states or which might promote or encourage the violence which could be so destructive to the freedom and the multicultural reality that we know here.
Separatism has a particular meaning for Canada. It reminds us of a very difficult period in our history. I think that most Canadians would strongly object to any other country giving support to anyone who promoted separatism in Canada, particularly through violent means. We would certainly press to have that country's government not give, or even be seen to give, any kind of support to such activities.

Mr. Speaker, The Sikh community has a long history in Canada. It has made an outstanding contribution to Canadian society, and as I said in the House on March 3: This House knows that the vast majority of Canadians of Sikh origin are first-class Canadian citizens trying to raise their families in peace and trying to raise their families in freedom. The Government has a duty to help them do so.

I have been privileged to visit Sikh temples in Toronto. I have met with representatives of the Sikh community across the country. I have also celebrated with them the richness of Sikh traditions which are enhanced so much when the adherents of Sikh traditions are free to practise their religion in peace. I also had the sad duty, as I told the House earlier, in June, 1986, of dedicating a memorial in Dunmanus Bay, Ireland, to the victims of the Air India tragedy, many of whom were Canadian Sikhs.
As I said in the House on March 3, "This House knows that the vast majority of Canadians of Sikh origin are first class Canadian citizens trying to raise their families in peace and trying to raise their families in freedom". The Government has a duty to help Canadians do that.
However, let us face the facts. The activities of a small, militant minority in the Sikh community represent the most serious internal security threat that Canada faces today. Undeniably this minority seeks to dismember a friendly
Supply
country, either through peaceful means or violent means. My friend, the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour), asked the other day whether there was not a difference between the World Sikh Organization and the other two. Indeed, Sir, there is a difference, but the constitution of the World Sikh Organization clearly states that one of its objectives is "to strive through peaceful means for the establishment of a Sikh nation, Khalistan". At the time that constitution was adopted there was a vigorous debate within the World Sikh Organization. They knew then that their decision would be controversial and the consequence of their decision is that their objectives are incompatible with Canadian policy.
Let me give you, Sir, some background on the other two organizations mentioned in my letter. The Babbar Khalsa is an India-based international organization comprising Sikhs whose objectives are the eradication of Sikh apostasy and the establishment of an independent state of Khalistan. In India the Babbar Khalsa has been involved in numerous acts of terror against moderate Sikhs, Hindus, and official representatives of the Government of India and its composite states. The Canadian branch is relatively small, but its total devotion to Sikh independence and its willingness to undertake acts of violence make it a serious source of concern.
In May, 1986, members of the Montreal area Canadian Babbar Khalsa were involved in a plot to place a bomb on an Air India flight from New York. Two were convicted and given life sentences. On May 25, 1986, four members of the ISYF attempted to assassinate a visiting Punjab state Minister in British Columbia. They were each sentenced to 20 years for this offence. As a Government, Sir, we cannot ignore these facts, nor can we ignore other cases of terrorism that we have encountered.
The International Sikh Youth Federation has its roots in the All India Sikh Student Federation, the largest and best organized Sikh extremist organization in India. The All India Sikh Student Federation activities and programs are directed toward disrupting and subverting the civil and political process in India for the express purpose of establishing an independent Sikh state of Khalistan. Members of that organization have been involved in aircraft hijackings, political assassinations, and the random, indiscriminate killings of both Sikh moderates and Hindus.
Moreover, these two organizations have occasionally attempted to dupe Members of Parliament or public figures in Canada into supporting their cause, for example, by having them photographed under the Khalistan flag or wearing buttons indicating support for Khalistan.
These groups exist largely to promote the creation of an independent Sikh state known as Khalistan based on the Indian state of Punjab. In pursuit of that objective some

March 10, 1988
Supply
members of that organization have used, counselled or promoted the use of violence.
The Canadian Government cannot remain silent when individuals or organizations advocate the use of violence for political ends, namely, the dismemberment of another country with which we have a longstanding and friendly relationship. My letter, therefore, asked our provincial Premiers to avoid appearing at organized events or activities which could inadvertently lend their endorsement to the separatist objectives of these groups.
My letter did not ask Premiers to avoid receiving or meeting with any particular individuals, whatever views they may espouse. Even though this Government rejects their separatist cause, we fully recognize all Canadians' right to freedom of expression. It is the attendance or participation by representatives of the Canadian people in events or functions sponsored by these three organizations about which I am concerned.
When political leaders openly associate with such groups, whether they intend to do so or not, they lend credence and support to the objectives for which those organizations stand. These organizations have in the past taken advantage of politicians attending their functions. I believe most Canadians would very strongly object and would want its government to object to another country's leaders giving support of any kind to anyone who promoted separatism in Canada, particularly through violent means. This Government would certainly press to have that country's government not give or even be seen to give any kind of support to such activities.
Naturally enough, such activities invite representations to the Government of Canada from the Government of India, just as Canada made representations to other countries in 1970 during the period of the FLQ. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs, I would be delinquent if I did not take account of the foreign policy implications, particularly for our relations with a friendly government on an issue which they regard as vital to their national integrity.
These activities also created deep concerns in Canada, particularly because the actions of a small minority are tearing the Canadian Sikh community apart. The point of concern and the reasons for sending my letter were activities within Canada. I act as a Canadian Minister in the interest of all Canadians.
As I said earlier, the activities of a small group of Sikhs in Canada constitutes one of the most serious internal security threats which Canada faces today. A militant minority in Canada has, through violence and intimidation, been able to exert a disproportionate influence in the community of Sikh origin in Canada.
[ Translation]
A number of initiatives have been taken by the Canadian Government to deal with the present situation so as to avoid any possibility of Canada becoming a centre of Sikh extremism.
Our most important initiative has been our attempt to express encouragement and support for moderate Sikhs who have decided to oppose the excesses of a militant minority that wants to wage, within our borders, a war that has its origins in another country.

Some have asked whether the Government has exercised its responsibility to warn public figures about other organizations in Canada. The answer is clearly yes, respecting the activities of groups which themselves, or through their members, are associated with violence or with the purpose of dismantling other friendly countries in Europe and elsewhere. I and my officials have received many inquiries from Members of Parliament and provincial governments about the nature and the objectives of groups which have requested meetings with public figures. We have provided the appropriate advice and have received co-operation in these instances.
The principle is the same. This is not a new policy. Other Canadian Governments have adopted similar positions. I note the presence in the House of the Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), the former Solicitor General. In addressing a comparable problem in 1984, he argued that acts of violence or terrorism in support of a free Armenia would not be tolerated in Canada and that this country should not become a surrogate battleground for alien causes. Rightly, he said that this would invite anarchy. He also said at the time that the efforts of the Government of the day, the Liberal Government in which he was a minister, were directed only at those who violate the laws of Canada. I would add that they should also be directed at those who counsel violation of our laws, directly or indirectly.
I said that the Government would be willing to provide briefings to Members of Parliament in camera. In that nonpartisan spirit, I must say that the External Affairs critic of the New Democratic Party has approached us. We have agreed to provide him with such a briefing. That option is open to other interested Members.
The real problem here is that whatever we might wish, Canada is not immune to violence and to terrorism. There have been too many instances of terrorism in this country. We, as the Government, have the responsibility to respond with firmness, within the bounds and the laws of a free and multicultural society. We owe that to all Canadians, but we owe it particularly to the great majority of Canadians of Sikh origin who are not, in a situation in which excessive pressures exist, free to pursue their goals in accordance with the traditions which drew them and so many to this country.
Where we are not doing enough as Members of the House of Commons is in reaching out to encourage the moderate majority of the Sikh community in Canada to stand strong against the tiny minority who practise or counsel terrorism or violence. We are having a debate today. I suggest to all Members of the House that the best next step for all Members would be to ensure and encourage the freedom of Canadians of
March 10, 1988

Sikh origin in this country to pursue their goals in Canada in accordance with their tradition and the laws of this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was delighted to be quoted by the Hon. Member and I stand exactly by everything the Member quoted. Does he not see a very great difference between the position of the former Government and the position which he has espoused? I was talking about breaking laws in Canada or advocating breaking laws elsewhere to achieve a separation in a country by violent means. It is one thing for us in this country to oppose international violence, it is quite another thing-and novel, I assert-for the Government of Canada to take sides on a question of separation where violent means are not the issue.
I will deal with the violence question in a moment because I think the Minister is wrong there as well. However, fundamentally, why does he believe that the Government of Canada should stand for any particular arrangement in a foreign country? Is it not for the Indians to determine the shape and the extent of their country? Is that not an issue on which people who are interested in India, wherever they are in the world, should be able to take a view and advocate by peaceful means? Why is the Government of Canada suddenly taking a position that the Conservative Government believes the present arrangements in different countries in the world are the correct ones?
The Armenian community of Canada, all of them proudly, and the overwhelming majority of them peacefully, would like to see a separate Armenia established partly in Turkey, which is a country with which we have an alliance. Does the Government of Canada not support listening to the Armenians and allowing members of the Canadian community to take sides on that question about whether or not there should be a separate Armenia? Again, we are not talking about violence.
Has the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) targeted the Armenian community for boycotting the Armenian Association that he knows well in Toronto? During the last election campaign his Cabinet colleagues visited them, made speeches and promises to them. What is wrong with people from a certain country wanting to see that country separate?
The Hon. Minister said, "We are opposed to the dismemberment of friendly states, particularly through violent means". I will agree that we are opposed to the dismemberment of friendly states through violent means. However, what about the dismemberment of friendly states through separatism, as a result of decisions the people of those countries might make and that Canadians with ties to that homeland might advocate? Why is the Minister introducing into the foreign policy of Canada the notion that we are committed to oppose the dismemberment of friendly states?
I can remember when I was a Minister and we were talking about the separation of Canada and fighting it. The United States let it be known, not through a formal statement but
Supply
clearly and unambiguously, that it wanted Canada to remain united. Was that helpful to us?
The point I want to make is why do countries which have friendly relations with another country feel that they have to take sides, for or against, concerning questions of separatism? Specifically, why does the Armenian community receive such different treatment from the Government than it is according to the Sikh community?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SIKH ORGANIZATIONS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the essential allegation is that this is a sudden policy or a new policy. It is not. The example that the Hon. Member used is the example that I will quote back to him. It was not very long ago when the Government of which he was a back-bench supporter in 1970 was dealing with the question of the FLQ and all of the consequences of that matter.
He has asked me if the expression by the United States of its belief in a united Canada was helpful to Canada. Let me put this question to him. What would the reaction of his friend, Pierre Elliott Trudeau, have been if the Government of the United States, through some of its senior members or through some of its leading parliamentarians, were to appear at meetings of the FLQ? What would be his reaction?
It is not an academic question since there was a position taken by the Government of Canada at that time.
The position that was taken by the Government of Canada at that time was based precisely upon the principle that I am invoking here.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SIKH ORGANIZATIONS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister has asked me a question. The FLQ was a terrorist organization. I challenge the Minister to characterize these organizations as terrorist organizations. He said that some members have promoted violence. Perhaps some members have. It has not been proven. But even if they have some members of a very large organization who may be promoting terrorism, that is a very unfair basis on which to characterize these organizations.
The Minister missed another point in the answer that he gave to me. He asked me how I would like it if the official position of the United States was for separation in Canada. I would not like the Americans to be for separation. I would not like them to be against it either. It is a matter for Canada. So when the United States takes an official position for or against it, it is stepping over the limit. That is my point.
For others, for provincial Premiers and for leading parliamentarians, surely a democracy such as India would understand that provincial premiers and leading parliamentarians are not the official voice of Canada. They are people who oppose in many cases the official voice of Canada.
Does the Secretary of State not see the difference between a country such as Canada taking a position for or against, which I think is quite wrong, and leading parliamentarians or provincial premiers being able to take positions? I am limiting this to the non-violent context because a terrorist organization,

as I indicated in my letter which was quoted by the Minister, is in a totally different situation.

Mr. Speaker, not to prolong this, to the best of my belief the position being articulated now by the Hon. Member is a position different from that followed in practice by the Government of which he was a supporter in 1970. Its concerns expressed to other countries did not relate exclusively to the FLQ but to the appearance of giving official support by countries friendly to Canada to separatist forces, however they were pursuing their goals within Canada. That is the answer to the best of my belief. I believe the record will prove that my recollection is correct.
The Hon. Member had a second question. I made a note of it, however, 1 regret to say, Mr. Speaker, that my writing becomes so illegible sometimes that I cannot understand it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SIKH ORGANIZATIONS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question on another tangent. The first words expressed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) in his remarks were with respect to an implication that I was exploiting for partisan gain this issue. I take offence to that. That offence does not come lightly. I take offence to that because 1 want to know why it is that whenever someone stands up in this Chamber and attempts to discuss or to defend a perceived injustice against a minority in our country the first response from the Government must always be that someone is trying to exploit for partisan gain.
I just want to put on the record that when one stands up for minorities it should not be construed as being for offensive, political partisan gain. The numbers are clearly not there to suggest that if one deals with perceptions one will necessarily gain politically from this issue. I point that out to the Minister quite honestly and candidly. The perception of political gain may be on the Government side. I allow the Minister those political gains.
What 1 am not prepared to say, Sir, is that it is fine to support one minority and to hold qualified support for another minority because that minority might not be as popular in this day and age. I refuse to subscribe to that qualified support for minorities. Either one is in favour of standing up for minorities or one is not.
I would like to ask the Minister this. He mentioned that members of a small militant group might be causing terrorist activities. I do not want it to be construed that we are sanctioning that small militant group, if in fact there is evidence to suggest that that is going on. There are 250,000 plus Canadians of Sikh origin. Some 20,000 Canadians of Sikh origin belong to the World Sikh Organization. There were 700 individuals who came out to a meeting on Sunday evening in my riding. It was attended by myself, the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata) and others. These people came out to the meeting partly because they had never met a Member of Parliament in their lives. They brought their wives, they did not leave them at home. They also brought their
children dressed in the costume of their nation. There were 700 people in a room that was meant to hold 500. Why in the name of goodness is the Minister trying to equate the membership of those organizations and that community with this type of letter?
I visited a city in our country just the other day where there were a number of municipal aldermen who were implicated in some wrongdoing in that city. The first question I was asked by a member of the media was, "Because you are of Italian extraction, Mr. Marchi, don't you feel a bit guilty or ashamed?" I said, "Why should I? I am not a municipal alderman in that city being implicated. Whether it is true or whether it is not is besides the point. Why should I feel ashamed? Why should my son or daughter carry that shame?" I suggested to this person that we have had individual Members of Parliament who have been implicated in wrongdoing. Is that to suggest that all Canadians of anglophone persuasion or of francophone persuasion ought to carry that shame? Of course not.
When will Canadians who are not from either French or English background cease to carry the shame of a few rather than having to carry the shame of an implication that is theirs by right through collectivity? The time has come to end that kind of thing.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SIKH ORGANIZATIONS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. The first point which the Hon. Member described as a tangent had to do with partisanship. His allegations, I reject.
The point that I meant to raise to my good friend, the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), was that naturally the people to whom I gave my considered advice are free to follow it or to reject it. They were owed, I believe, my considered judgment, and they have received it.
Third, as I mentioned in my remarks, the World Sikh Organization itself in debating its constitution spent a great deal of time discussing whether or not there would be a reference in that constitution to the independent state of Khalistan. They knew the controversy at the time that that constitution was debated.
Fourth, a large part of our purpose here is to try to create a set of circumstances in which that great majority of Canadians of Sikh origin will in fact be free to pursue their own values in this country and not be subject to the types of pressures that we all know exist now and that impose a very real burden on them.
Finally, Sir, on a matter of apology, I advise my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) that,
March 10, 1988

unfortunately, I am due to be hosting a luncheon for Lord Peter Carrington at precisely this moment. I know the profound interest of my friend, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, and he would not want me to be absent from the lunch. 1 normally try to stay in the House on debates in which I am involved, but I cannot in these circumstances.
Mir. Nelson A. Riis (Kamloops-Shuswap): Mr. Speaker, I must say that this is not a happy day for myself, and I suspect for most if not all Members of Parliament, to have to chastise the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) on a particular initiative that he has decided to launch.
It is sad because this is a very dark day for the Canadian Sikh community; a quarter million Canadians of the Sikh culture and the Sikh faith are wounded as the result of the decision of the Secretary of State for External Affairs to suggest to Canadians that certain Sikh organizations are not worthy of a visit by a Member of Parliament, or others.
It is a dark day for the Sikh community when the Secretary of State draws attention to what he states are inappropriate actions on behalf of certain Sikh organizations and, in a sense, it casts a pall over the entire Sikh community. Today a dark cloud hangs over the Sikh community of Canada which simply fans the fires of discrimination and racism that we see glimpses of today. The sad part about it is that it should never have happened. While I applaud a number of initiatives undertaken by the Secretary of State on behalf of our country, this is not one of them. His initiative was wrong. His condemnation of the World Sikh Organization was completely and totally inappropriate.
I speak for my colleagues in the New Democratic Party who have a long history of speaking out in support of minority groups in Canada. The history of Sikhs in Canada has not always been an easy one. From their origins before the turn of the century when the first Sikhs entered Canada to become some of the most exemplary groups of Canadians that we have ever witnessed, they have encountered difficulties. In 1908 the Government of Canada banned Sikh migration. In 1914 during the Kamagata Maru incident nearly 400 Sikhs who had indicated an interest in journeying to Canada to become citizens were stopped at the Port of Vancouver and through a Canadian gun ship were eventually forced to return to India.
In an effort to remind ourselves of this incredibly black incident, I have a Private Member's Motion that, if passed by the House, would see the erection of a memorial cairn on the West Coast to remind us that certain groups of Canadians have had a difficult time in our country. We ought to go out of our way, as parliamentarians, and the Government of Canada ought to go out of its way, to ensure that all Canadians are treated fairly, and that as a result of a Government initiative no Canadian ought to feel any sense of discrimination, harassment, or feel any of the pangs of racist activity.
Supply
Sikhs have assisted Canada in its development in the forest industry, in agriculture, in commerce, in the professions, and as I stated earlier, Sikhs have become exemplary citizens in virtually every walk of life. One of the reasons that Sikhs were attracted to our country and have assisted in its development can be found in what Canada is and what it represents in the world nations. This is a country that prides itself on its multicultural policies, and its Charter of Rights and Freedoms. There is a section in our Constitution that states that Canadians will have the freedom of conscience and religion; Canadians will have the freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression, and Canadians will have the freedom of peaceful assembly. That is what members of the World Sikh Organization thought existed in Canada.
In the constitution and by-laws of the World Sikh Organization there are a number of objectives, for example:
To promote and facilitate an active line of communication amongst the Sikhs of the world.
To promote and protect Sikh interests all over the world by participating in the formulation and implementation of the policies of the Sikh nation.
To work for the promotion of the ideals of universal brotherhood, peace, justice, freedom of worship and speech, respect for cultural diversity and human dignity for all, without any distinction as per the instruments and covenants of the United Nations' Organization.
And this, Mr. Speaker, is the important one:
To strive through peaceful means, for the establishment of a Sikh nation, Khalistan, in order to protect the Sikh identity and faith as ordained by Guru Panth in the daily prayer 'Raj Karega Khalsa'.
I wish to emphasize the words "peaceful means". In the very statement of objectives of the World Sikh Organization, the organization indicates that it will work through peaceful means.
The Secretary of State has indicated that he was concerned about terrorism and violence. All parliamentarians oppose terrorism of any type. All parliamentarians oppose the use of terrorism in terms of fostering any peaceful action. Whether it is terrorism by Canadians or on Canadian soil or elsewhere, it must be opposed.
The manner in which this is opposed is by Governments encouraging peaceful political action, peaceful protest, and peaceful discussion. Therefore, I believe that encouragement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the seven Premiers to whom he wrote hampers peaceful political pursuits of any multicultural organization. It contradicts his goal of fighting terrorism.
Many of us have attended meetings of the World Sikh Organization. Many of us who have gurdwaras in our own communities know members of the World Sikh Organization and have good friends who are members of that organization. We take some offence to the letter that the Secretary of State for External Affairs sent to seven Premiers. We take offence for two reasons. The first is that the Secretary of State for External Affairs did not feel it was appropriate to send the same information to Members of Parliament, did not feel it was appropriate to send the same information to the Leaders

March 10, 1988
Supply
of the opposition Parties in the House of Commons, and felt it was not appropriate or necessary to send the same letter to mayors and councils of the metropolitan areas of Canada, some of which represent millions of Canadians.
I want to read from the letter which was sent to the seven Premiers. In part the Secretary of State for External Affairs wrote:
I would appreciate your co-operation in avoiding events and activities which
could be perceived as supporting the Sikh organizations mentioned above or
their objective in the creation of an independent Sikh state.
Of course one organization mentioned was the World Sikh Organization. What goes on in the country of India is of little interest to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, or at least it ought to be. It is a concern of the Government of India. Whether or not the political organizations of India in terms of territory are appropriate is not for the Government of Canada to hold a view on; it is a matter for the Government of India.
The fact that there are Canadian citizens, people living in Canada, who have personal views about the need for a country such as Khalistan ought to be of little concern to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. These are Canadian citizens who, by our Constitution, have the right to hold whatever views they wish to hold in terms of having the freedom of thought, belief, opinion, and expression. I must also remind the Secretary of State for External Affairs that Canadians have the freedom of peaceful assembly to discuss matters of concern to them, whatever they may be.
In terms of history, I recall Canadian citizens who had concerns regarding the eventual formation of the State of Israel and Canadians today of Palestinian origin who are interested in the creation of a homeland for Palestinians. They have meetings and discuss the matter. I also recall Slovaks, Croatians, and Ukrainians living in Canada who have an interest in the creation of homelands for their peoples.
The fact that the Secretary of State for External Affairs would single out this particular incident, take sides with a foreign country, and say that we support the position of the Government of India against the views held by Canadian citizens is completely and totally inappropriate.
What we see here, in a sense, is group condemnation. When we single out an organization, such as the World Sikh Organization with membership in the tens of thousands, and recognize that across Canada our friends and colleagues are members of the World Sikh Organization and therefore, by implication, are condemned by the Secretary of State for External Affairs for harbouring terrorist notions and supporting violence and terrorism, it is completely inappropriate. This collective guilt which the Secretary of State for External Affairs has created, this group guilt or group condemnation, is completely unacceptable.
He went on to indicate in his letter that members of these organizations had also engaged in or promoted violent activities. I want to remind him that organizations do not carry out violent activities; individuals do. If the Secretary of State for External Affairs has information that people are participating in violent activities, arranging terrorist activities or participating in terrorist activities, then we should take the appropriate steps and lay charges. We should deal with these individuals as individuals in Canada, but not condemn an entire organization and, by implication, an entire community in Canada.
The Sikh community is grieving today. It is being torn apart and is being ghettoized in a community sense because of the sweeping generalization and sweeping condemnation of the Secretary of State for External Affairs as a result of the letter. If he has evidence that indeed terrorism is being encouraged, that terrorist activities are being organized, and that violence is occurring as a result of some organizations, let him take action and provide evidence.
I listened very carefully to his words today. There was not a shred of evidence, not a single fact which would give his initiative any credibility. It is easy to stand and condemn a group of innocent people but, quite frankly, that activity has no place in a free and democratic society.
It seems that the only appropriate action now would be to clear the air. I am very saddened by the fact that the matter will now have to go to some form of inquiry, but I think it is the only alternative left. This means that the issue will stay on the front pages of newspapers and be reiterated time and time again in the news media, which will lead to more and more of a cloud over this very critical, important, and integral community in Canada.
Whether that is done through the appropriate standing committees of the House of Commons, whether the matter is referred to the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism, to the Standing Committee on Human Rights, to the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General, or to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade, I do not think is particularly critical, as long as the Secretary of State for External Affairs is called upon either to provide evidence or to apologize to the Sikh community of Canada and to the organizations he has named in his letter. If he does not, it will be up to the Sikh community to take action, because I believe that there is no way the Sikh community can stand condemned by the Secretary of State for External Affairs without fighting back for its rights.
It is sad that this must take place in a free and democratic country like Canada. Of course its initiatives can take the form of hearings through the Canadian Human Rights Commission or the form of court actions to clear the names of the World Sikh Organization and the other named organizations.
It seems puzzling that the whole matter has occurred. I would like to think that it has no relationship at all to our trade relationship with India. Indian government representatives in Canada have dissociated themselves totally from the initiative taken by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. They say that in no way did they urge the Minister to take this
March 10, 1988

initiative, that in no way did they counsel the Minister that this was appropriate or necessary. It was simply something done by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, presumably on his own decision. It is puzzling, because I recall attending meetings and conventions of various Sikh organizations where there were representatives of the government Party in attendance and where members of Cabinet sent greetings and so on, presumably endorsing the goals of the organization or their efforts in Canada.
The fact that the World Sikh Organization has as one of its goals the creation of an independent Sikh homeland, does not mean that a Member of Parliament attending a meeting of that organization necessarily supports that particular initiative or particular goal. I notice that the Secretary of State for External Affairs meets regularly with representatives of the South African Government. Presumably that does not mean that the Government of Canada supports apartheid. I could think of a number of public meetings or public gatherings of organizations which I attended. That would certainly not mean that I support all their goals and objectives.
Actually, we as a Parliament must go beyond simply clearing the air on this particular issue. We also have to take other actions. We have to take action in our immigration offices. We have to take action in our customs offices. We have to take action through CSIS and the RCMP and through our High Commissioner in India. I am sure all Members of Parliament who have Sikhs in their communities could identify countless examples of discrimination against Sikhs, discrimination against Canadian citizens who we know very well and work alongside, but who happen to be different because their name is Singh and because they are members of the Sikh organization.
I heard of a sad situation the other day. A gentleman, was crossing the border coming from the United States into Canada. A Sikh was accompanying him. As he was stopped at the border the customs officer looked into the vehicle and said, "That's fine, Sir. You can go through. But we will have to question this associate of yours". When asked why the officer said, "We are under orders to do that". Presumably the only difference was that one man had a turban and one man did not, one man's name included the word Singh and the other one did not. One was a Sikh and the other was not. Because of the ability of the customs officer to identify the individual's cultural heritage meant that he would be interrogated because there were orders to do so. In a country that prides itself on its freedom, its multicultural heritage and policy, whose government puts out a report called "Equality Now", we cannot tolerate that kind of discrimination at our borders.
We all know of individual immigration cases that we work on. Again, there are subtle ways of discriminating against people of the Sikh faith. The Secretary of State for External Affairs must provide a forum in which to justify his particular behaviour in this instance, or he must apologize to the World
Supply
Sikh Organization and to the Sikhs of Canada. It is now obligatory for the Government to take a number of other actions, as I said earlier, with our customs officials, our Immigration departments, in New Delhi through the High Commissioner's office, with the police and with CSIS to ensure that appropriate missives are communicated. Discrimination against those of the Sikh faith cannot be tolerated and the Sikhs in Canada should be able to play their rightful role as Canadian citizens.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SIKH ORGANIZATIONS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the remarks of the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) of the New Democratic Party. I think he made some very valid points. I would like to dwell on freedom of expression and freedom of association. I think it is a fundamental right for Canadians to have this freedom. Our Charter guarantees that freedom to all Canadians. What bothers me about the whole situation is that in trying to influence other members of governments whether provincial or federal, telling them that they can or should not attend certain functions, is contrary to the fundamental principle of Canadian justice and the Charter.
Does the Hon. Member believe that we as Canadians have to uphold the fundamental principles of the Charter, the freedom of expression and the freedom of association?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SIKH ORGANIZATIONS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the intervention of my hon. colleague from Calgary. Yes, not only must we take steps to ensure that the rights and freedoms of Canadians are upheld, but perhaps we should go beyond that and take extraordinarily steps at times to ensure that no Canadian is ever left with the impression that his or her rights are less than others.
This particular issue gives us that opportunity. We have heard from Members on all sides of this House. The matter has cut across partisan political lines. We have heard from Members of the Liberal Party, Members of the Conservative Party and Members of the New Democratic Party condemning the Secretary of State for External Affairs for inappropriate action, for an action, if you like, that virtually encourages terrorist activities. It works against people expressing their views in an open and free way.
There is another fundamental right that we as parliamentarians have to be particularly sensitive to, namely, being asked not to attend certain kinds of functions. We all have the intelligence to decide what groups we are prepared to discuss issues with and what organizations we are prepared to meet with. We do not need a lecture from the Secretary of State for External Affairs to indicate to Members of Parliament which are or are not appropriate groups.
When it comes to domestic affairs in India, that is the concern of the Indian Government. Our Secretary of State for External Affairs, I think, would be spending his time more appropriately taking steps to ensure that the rights and freedoms of Canadians are being upheld as opposed to being, if

March 10, 1988
you like, a voice, which in this case, obviously was for another Government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SIKH ORGANIZATIONS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I want to commend my colleague from British Columbia on a very well thought and articulated representation in the House on this sensible issue. I applaud the courage and the decency of stating one's convictions, which the Hon. Member for Calgary East (Mr. Kindy) did. I am pleased that the House Leader for the New Democratic Party has signalled publicly his support for the appropriate forum and inquiry, as difficult as it will be for the community and for the Canadian fabric, to try to clear the air on this issue. Hopefully we will get the Government to concede on that point, notwithstanding that the Secretary of State for External Affairs did not refuse or agree to such an inquiry. I hope my submission to the Standing Committee on Multicul-turalism, which was one of the committees mentioned by the NDP House Leader, will be successful in trying to evaluate that evidence which is currently confidential and in the possession of the Government.
Could the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) tell us why the Prime Minister of Canada would send his congratulations, recognition and best wishes publicly on June 7 to the World Sikh Organization meeting in his own province while probably at the same time-the letter was dated December 7 and as the Member knows it takes quite a bit of time to consider action, write a letter and redraft it-secretly the Government was making moves in the very opposite direction from the public endorsation of the Prime Minister?

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, once again the Tibetan people are demanding their independence and freedom. It has now been 38 years since China marched into Tibet to enforce its rule on this small, peaceful country, and it is 29 years since the uprising of Tibetans on March 10, 1959, to protest the foreign domination of their country.
