subtopic: REASSESSMENT OF USED FARM MACHINERY TRADE-IN PRICES
REASSESSMENT OF USED FARM MACHINERY TRADE-IN PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, would any MP in this House like to have his or her income tax reassessed because Revenue Canada deemed that a garage allowed too high a sum for a used auto that was traded in three years ago? No, not one.
That is what some farmers who traded used farm machines in on new ones three or four years ago are facing. In effect, Revenue officials are asking our farmers to change the figures on bills of sale. If a company allowed too much for the used machine, why should the farmer be responsible?
All of us, and probably all Canadians, get as much as possible for used machines when buying new ones. If the company pays too much, it has the God-given right to go broke, but the farmer should not now be reassessed because some ridiculous regulation was promoted by a bureaucrat who thinks he knows more about the price of farm equipment than the farmer or the manufacturer. I urge the Minister to rescind this ridiculous regulation and to stop his officials from harassing our farmers.
March 10, 1988

subtopic: SUGGESTION PROJECTS IMPROVING WOMEN'S LIVING CONDITIONS BE EMPHASIZED
SUGGESTION PROJECTS IMPROVING WOMEN'S LIVING CONDITIONS BE EMPHASIZED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in Africa where 80 per cent of the people live in rural areas, women do about 70 per cent of the work. Yet traditionally, aid funding has gone to men. Training has been provided for men despite the fact that women actually do the job. Women in developing countries need more training and land ownership, more equality in access to credit, and more legal protection.
The Government recently released a strategy paper which read in part:
Women are half the world's population but they put in two-thirds of its work
hours, receive one-tenth of its income and own less than one-hundredth of its
property.
The strategy paper states that CIDA supports grassroots projects developed by and for women.
Another new report by the North-South Institute presents an overview of NGO activity under the title "Bridges of Hope". It points out that in only 33 per cent of projects were local women actually involved in project design.
We must assure Canadians that the larger percentage of money going to NGOs and businesses will be dependent to some extent on the degree to which projects improve the living conditions of women.

subtopic: INITIATIVE TO STOP DRUG ABUSE IN PENITENTIARIES
INITIATIVE TO STOP DRUG ABUSE IN PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this week the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) made an important announcement at an international conference on substance abuse. He stated that both CSC and RCMP have launched a joint initiative to fight the flow of drugs both into and within prisons. The Minister has to be congratulated for his leadership and for his important contribution to the National Drug Strategy.
As a member of the legal and justice committee, I have visited many institutions over the last few months and have met many inmates. As Hon. Members are aware, the process of rehabilitating inmates is much more difficult when drugs are readily available. I can assure Hon. Members that the step taken by the Solicitor General is one that will really help those who want to be rehabilitated.
Fewer drugs in prisons will result in a more sound environment for inmates and prison workers, as well as a safer place within which to work. As a Canadian citizen and as a father, I am proud of the Minister's initiative. It provides Canadians
with a safer society to live in and sets a good example for all citizens to follow.

Mr. Speaker, the people of Montreal are becoming increasingly impatient with the federal Government's failure to act decisively on projects as important as the development of the Vieux-Port and the space agency.
We all remember that in November 1986, the Committee chaired by Mr. Laurent Picard made these projects its two main recommendations for reviving the economy of Greater Montreal. Unfortunately, on December 2 the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. de Cotret) responded to these recommendations with some well-meaning platitudes, and two days later, all those representing Montreal's socioeconomic and political interests deplored this lack of decisive action.
Mr. Speaker, the people of Montreal want to know what the federal Government intends to do about the space agency. Is the federal Government going to announce its decision before, during or after the election campaign, which means never?

subtopic: THREE-WHEEL ALL-TERRAIN VEHICLES NEEDED IN NORTHERN REGIONS
THREE-WHEEL ALL-TERRAIN VEHICLES NEEDED IN NORTHERN REGIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Transport Canada has suspended the sale of three-wheel all-terrain vehicles in Canada, following as usual the lead of the United States. The suspension may be acceptable in the provinces where roads have been developed, and the suspension is enforced in areas where the vehicles cannot be used anyway. However, in the Keewatin and central Arctic regions, where there is a lot of tundra and muskeg, the three-wheel ATVs are less expensive than the four-wheel versions, and are used extensively for hunting and for work.
Northerners have already been hit hard financially by the anti-fur lobby. Forcing them to buy four-wheel ATVs instead of three-wheel ATVs imposes a further financial burden because the price difference can be as much as $1,000 to $3,000.

March 10, 1988
Suspension of the three-wheel ATVs was opposed by all the callers to a territorial open-line program held at Rankin Inlet last Friday. Therefore, I urge the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) to allow the sale of the three-wheel version to northern residents until roads have been built.

subtopic: TRANSPORTATION OF PLUTONIUM-AMENDMENT OF UNITED STATES-JAPAN AGREEMENT
TRANSPORTATION OF PLUTONIUM-AMENDMENT OF UNITED STATES-JAPAN AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last year the U.S. and Japanese Governments signed a nuclear agreement calling for possible transportation of plutonium, a speck of which can cause cancer, over Canada. Canadians did not like this idea and said so.
From Arctic Bay to Eskimo Point to Iqualit, to Whitehorse, to Toronto, to Faro, to Edmonton, to Vancouver and to Haines Junction in the Yukon, and in many other communities, thousands of Canadians signed petitions to this Parliament opposing those flights. Letters were sent to Canadian and American government officials. NDP and Liberal MPs demanded answers. The Canadian and U.S. media followed the issue closely.
Tad Homer-Dixon, a Canadian student at Massachusetts Institute of Technology, worked to oppose these flights. John Polanyi, Nobel Prize winner, spoke out in opposition.
For those cynics who say ordinary persons cannot make a difference, here is proof positive that they can. We have learned through the U.S. Department of State that the U.S.-Japan nuclear agreement will be modified through an official exchange of letters requiring the Japanese to pursue an allwater route.
There are still concerns. Nuclear proliferation is a real threat. There are environmental dangers. The fight is not over but we can be pleased that we, ordinary people, have won a major battle.

subtopic: INCREASE IN GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS OF WOMEN
INCREASE IN GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS OF WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we mark the end of International Women's Week it is appropriate to bring to light the dramatic progress this Government has made in appointing women to key decision-making positions.
We have almost doubled the percentage of women appointed to federal boards, agencies and commissions. The figure now stands at 28.6 per cent, compared to 15 per cent under the previous Government.
The number of federally appointed women judges has risen to 20, a 22 per cent increase since our Government took office. Appointments of women to senior levels in the federal Public Service have more than doubled.
Twelve women have been appointed to positions as Ambassadors, High Commissioners, and Consuls General, a rate six times higher than that of the previous Government.
This is not a token gesture but clear evidence of this Government's recognition of the talents and competence of Canadian women.
Mr. Speaker, he finally did it.
Did what?
He threw in the towel.
Who?

I am glad the Hon. Member asked. Jean Sirois, of course. Jean Sirois, the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) friend, Tory bagman, leadership supporter of the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald), an all-round Tory, has decided that he no longer wants a juicy $64,000 a year political appointment as Chairman of Telefilm Canada, effective April 13. He wants to go back to his law business where he can make the real dough, such as $400,000 legal contracts which he recently got from the federal Government and his friend, the Prime Minister.
Canadians are relieved that Jean Sirois is leaving. He has long since worn out his welcome at Telefilm Canada. However, we want to know why April 13. The Prime Minister should phone him up today and tell him to leave the keys to the executive washroom before he goes home tonight.

Mr. Speaker, why wait until spring? I say we should fire Jean Sirois as of now!

Mr. Speaker, in December, 1986, a list of communities qualifying
March 10, 1988

for northern resident tax benefits was released by the Department of Finance. Surprisingly, the list included several villages in southwestern Saskatchewan. Because it is manifestly unfair that residents of one community qualify for the tax benefit while those all around it do not, I raised the matter in this House on several occasions in April of 1987, requesting revision of the criteria used in designating an isolated post. Unfortunately, the subsequent revisions merely exacerbated the problem by confirming the original list, while excluding all other communities.
The determination procedure is arbitrary, inequitable, and capricious, and requires urgent attention. I call on the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to act quickly by putting a senior person in charge of drafting common sense criteria which ensure that all residents of an area are treated fairly, evenly, and consistently.

Mr. Speaker, last week a senior immigration official spoke about foreign domestic workers as follows:
So what we have is a half-way house, really. We bring them in, and if they prove that they are good at their job then we land them and then they can stay in that job if they want or go on to something else. But at least they have two years in which they have to stay .with the family and do what we ask them to do. In the old system, when we brought them in just as immigrants, they would never stay. They would do day work, but they would never live in the house and stay, because they are out of their environment with the people of their own group.
Half-way houses are for unfortunates such as prisoners being rehabilitated, or ex-psychiatric patients, or the mentally retarded. It is wrong to speak so paternalistically about the hundreds of women, mostly Caribbean or Filipino, who come to work hard as domestics for Canadian families. Their pay is often shockingly low and they are often treated very badly. Federal or provincial laws or unions give them almost no protection. Canada needs these domestic workers. Immigration workers ought not to insult them.

subtopic: SUPREME COURT DECISION-CALL FOR LEGISLATION TO RESPECT HUMAN LIFE
SUPREME COURT DECISION-CALL FOR LEGISLATION TO RESPECT HUMAN LIFE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Supreme Court of Canada's decision of January 28, 1988, has
left the country without an abortion law. It is now possible for abortion to take place any time during the nine months after conception.
We must, as parliamentarians, move quickly to remedy this deplorable situation. Nothing in the Supreme Court of Canada's decision establishes abortion as a right. We must, therefore, find a way to give both mothers and children the right to life and freedom.
Accordingly, we must bring in legislation which respects human life at all stages of development. A human foetus in the womb at three weeks is just as valuable to society and as much human as an unborn child at 24 weeks.
On this, the great moral question of the 20th century, all Members of Parliament must state clearly where they stand on the question of life or death for unborn children. I am proud to stand with those millions of Canadians who condemn the present situation. I join their plea for protection of unborn children.

subtopic: FINANCING OF PREGNANCY INTERRUPTION AND FREEDOM OF CHOICE-POSITION OF BRITISH COLUMBIA SOCIAL CREDIT MEMBER OF LEGISLATURE
FINANCING OF PREGNANCY INTERRUPTION AND FREEDOM OF CHOICE-POSITION OF BRITISH COLUMBIA SOCIAL CREDIT MEMBER OF LEGISLATURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I want to congratulate Miss Kim Campbell, Social Credit MLA in British Columbia, for having had the courage of her convictions.
Yesterday, Miss Campbell openly defied Premier Vander Zalm by saying she supported public financing for abortions and freedom of choice for women. "I am not for sale", said Miss Campbell.
Mr. Speaker, I admire and respect the stand she has taken. In fact, isn't this what politics is all about: Having the courage of one's own and one's constituents' convictions, whatever the political cost?
Premier Vander Zalm has publicly ignored the will of the majority of the voters in his province and has rejected the wisdom of the Supreme Court.
Miss Campbell is to be commended for her integrity and honesty. By her actions she has strengthened the democratic process, speaking up for those whose views are being ignored by Mr. Vander Zalm.

March 10, 1988
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, the Charter is diluting democracy in Canada. We now have two kinds of government, the elected government of Parliament and the unelected government of judges. The elected government proposes, the unelected government disposes.
The fault with this does not lie in the quality of decisions. The recent decision of British Columbia was right in my judgment. The fault lies in the way that the ultimate authority is no longer the elected government and, therefore, the ultimate authority is no longer the electors it represents.
This subject will not command the headlines or the television news. It has no quick fix, but it is fundamental to the future of democracy in Canada and it should be on the forward planning agenda of Parliament.

subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND-ELECTION OF LIBERAL IN PROVINCIAL BYELECTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I note that it is 2.15 and I am delighted because many Members are here to hear the good news. It has been nearly four decades since Newfoundland joined Confederation, nearly 40 years. In all of those 40 years the constituents of Waterford-Kenmount, which riding in the area of St. John's West previously went by other names, had always voted Conservative.
Wednesday night, in the middle of the riding of St. John's West, the riding of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), the people of Waterford-Kenmount returned a Liberal, with a huge shot in the arm for the Liberal Party of Newfoundland. This is equivalent to the Riverview win in New Brunswick.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, as night follows day this means that the Liberal Party in Newfoundland and Labrador is on its way to government. I know that the Member for St. John's West, the Minister of Transport, joins me in congratulating Mr. Eric Gullage, the brand new Member in his federal riding, for a job well done and for the beginning of a brand new Liberal Government in the Province of Newfoundland and Labrador.

subtopic: CENTRES OF EXCELLENCE-SUGGESTED EXPANSION INTO NETWORK CONCEPT
CENTRES OF EXCELLENCE-SUGGESTED EXPANSION INTO NETWORK CONCEPT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) January announcement that Canada would spend an additional $1.3 billion on research and development and would foster the establishment of centres of excellence has been enthusiastically received by the research community, and stimulated much discussion around the centres of excellence concept.
Perhaps this should be expanded into "networks of excellence". This is the view of Professor Gilles Barbery, Director of Mines and Metallurgy at Laval University. His field of research is one in which Canada ought naturally to excel. It is, however, shared by several universities, business corporations, and both provincial and federal government research establishments such as CANMET. Instead of centering all research in a specific geographical location we should strengthen the network, each component of which could develop its own speciality.
The same of course is true for other areas of research such as medicine, communications, or space technology.

subsubtopic: CAPE BRETON DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION-PICTOU COUNTY COAL MINE PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, the Minister responsible for the operations of the Cape Breton Development Corporation. The Minister will know of a document which was submitted to the Government of Canada and the Government of Nova Scotia in December of 1987 with regard to the new coal mine for Pictou County. The document said that DEVCO's board of directors believe that they have a duty to respectfully advise both levels of government of DEVCO's considered opinion that a deep coal mine in Pictou County would not give benefit to Nova Scotia's economy, and that the impact such a mine would have upon the province's existing coal industry would offset any benefit.
I would ask the Minister whether or not he agrees with that particular opinion, since he and his Government appointed the senior management of DEVCO as well as the members of the board of directors.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Thousands of Canadian small businesses and indeed hundreds of thousands of Canadians are grateful that we have seen a drop of 360 bases points in interest rates since the Government has come to office, and nearly 1,300 bases points since the height of 22 per cent interest rates under the previous Government. However, in light of the very strong dollar, there still remains a 2 per cent gap between interest rates in Canada and those in the United States. I wonder if the Minister can explain why we do not see interest rates dropping more these days.

Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member has pointed out, interest rates have come down quite considerably since we took office. I should point out that he has made one comparison between interest rates in Canada and those in the United States. If he were to look at the prime bank rate of the two countries, I believe he would see that the gap is 1.25 per cent.
I have indicated and the Governor of the Bank of Canada has indicated that we are watching this very closely. We do have some concerns about the incipient inflationary pressure and we want to make sure that we deal with that now, rather than allow it to become a major problem in the future. This is contrary to what had been done in the past. In 1981-82 we saw the results of that inactivity. That is the basis of the interest rate policies of the Government of Canada, but I do appreciate the concern the Hon. Member has expressed, and we will be watching it very closely.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SIKH ORGANIZATIONS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am anxious to participate in the debate today on the motion put forward by the Official Opposition. We have put forward this resolution because we want to bring to the attention of the Canadian people and the Government that a policy has been introduced by the Government which amounts to nothing less than a betrayal of the policy of multiculturalism. It is also a violation of the rights of free speech and free association, not just of the Sikh community which is the target for the Secretary of State for External Affairs' attack, but of all minority groups and all ethnic groups.
I participated in the debate earlier today when I had the opportunity to have some exchanges with the Minister. In the 20 minutes I have to participate now I want to deal with two questions in the context of this outrageous letter from the Minister. First, what is the proper role for the Government of Canada in the face of some or all members of any ethnic community espousing as a cause the separation of all or part of their historic homeland from its present arrangements? What attitude should the Government take toward that situation? Second, how is that affected by the intrusion of violence or unlawful means to effect that end?
The advocacy and promotion of separation in any part of the world can be democratic. When we are looking at the question, we ought to give that the first look. Then we should turn to how the position of the Government of Canada should be affected when it appears that violence or other unlawful means are associated with the cause.
The Minister made clear the position of his Government on that question. There is not much doubt about it. He said the official government position is to oppose the dismemberment or dismantling of friendly states, and then he added, "particularly through violent means". I will deal with that, but let us just deal with the dismemberment of friendly states.
I do not think it ought to be the official position of the Government of Canada, and I insist it has not been in the past, that Canada was in favour of or opposed to dismemberment of any particular state by peaceful, lawful means. Surely that is an issue for the people in the country concerned to decide. They have to decide on the shape and extent of their nation. However, here is the important additional point. People living in Canada have a right to their views about the situation in other countries, whether they are elected or not. That has
nothing to do with the official position of the Government of Canada which, as I say, should be neither for nor against. Within our country, I argue that the people have the right to have views, to promote their views, to advocate their views, peacefully, lawfully, as to the separation or otherwise of some other country.
The Minister made one particularly outrageous statement in his remarks and I want to explore it. I will give the House the tenor of the statement because I do not have the exact words in front of me. He said the vast majority of Sikhs want to come to Canada to live their lives peacefully. The implication was that they did not want to have anything to do with the situation in the homeland. He could be right about that; maybe the majority do, maybe some do, but that is their business. However, the idea that somehow or other it is wrong for them to have views about the arrangements in their historic homeland is so fundamentally offensive to our notion of multiculturalism that it has to be challenged right here in this place. The Government of Canada has no business suggesting that nice boys and girls who come to this country from another country should live their lives in Canada with nothing to say and nothing to think about their historic homeland. Just to put the proposition is to show how offensive it is.
People come to this country from many troubled places in the world. They bring all kinds of baggage with them including how they feel about the way their country is developing, their relatives, and their former fellow citizens, or perhaps their present fellow citizens because they may continue, under the laws of Canada, to remain citizens of both countries. Mr. Clark is telling the multicultural communities of this country-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SIKH ORGANIZATIONS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Order. I would like to bring to the attention of this long-term Member, who knows better, that he should not be using the Minister's name.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SIKH ORGANIZATIONS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rarely as outraged as I am by this and I apologize to you for referring to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) by his surname.
He is telling these people to come to Canada, to make this their homeland, to bring us their ideas, their songs, their dances, and their dishes, but not to open their baggage. He is telling them to leave their suitcases closed, to lock them up in their cupboards and not to start bringing out the things which bothered them when they were living in their historic homeland.
What nonsense that is. It is completely unacceptable to limit multicultural communities to living their lives in Canada now, to tell them that now that they are in Canada they must be good boys and girls and forget about the problems in the part of the world from which they came.
Well, Mr. Secretary of State for External Affairs, the communities which come to Canada are entitled to have their
March 10, 1988

views, to form associations, and to express their views without being told that that is somehow un-Canadian and without having officials of the Government of Canada, elected officials, and provincial premiers warned not to visit a group because it espouses the dismantlement of a friendly state.
We know something about the possibilities of separation in our country; we lived with that. It is always a possibility on the horizon of any great federal state that there will be a movement which will want to separate. What attitude should countries that are friendly to Canada take? Should they take the view that Canada has no business going through a debate about separation, that they are in favour of our country remaining united, or the opposite?
I draw a distinction between the official position of a country and the position of other elected people in the country or other prominent opinion leaders in the country. The official position should be neutral. When the President of France came to Canada and said "Vive le Quebec libre" meaning "I, France, am in favour of Quebec being an independent country" he was kicked out, and quite rightly, because he was speaking for France. He was the head of a country visiting our country and taking sides. That is wrong. However, to suggest that members of the French society should not have views on whether Canada should be separate or together, or advocate or promote them, is a totally different thing. I urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs to reconsider that position and to return to the traditional view that we do not take sides on the shape or extent of nations, friendly or unfriendly.
The Minister has picked on the Sikhs who are, unfortunately, the targets of a lot of criticism in this country, undeservedly so as far as the vast majority are concerned. What about the Armenians who live in Canada? They advocate the separation of that part of Turkey and the Soviet Union and the creation of an independent state. What about the Ukrainians? Do you think that Ukrainian Canadians are happy watching the nationalism of their homeland being snuffed out? Do you think they must remain silent about it and that no Ministers or Members of Parliament should listen to the aspirations of Ukrainian Canadians to have their historic homeland returned to an independent country? There are the Croations, the Basques in Spain, the Estonians, the Lithuanians, and the Latvians. The list is endless. For the Government of Canada to tell all of those ethnic groups to keep their baggage closed if they want to be considered good Canadians, not to let out these ideas which make certain foreign powers uncomfortable, is not the Canadian way to handle irredentism, to handle separatist aspirations or democratic nationalistic aspirations which multicultural communities have.
There are some rules. This type of recognition can create some tensions in our country. There is no doubt that it can. However, we fortunately have some rules for guiding the debate in our country. They do not include the kind of smarmy letter, to which I referred earlier, which the Secretary of State
Supply
for External Affairs had the crust to read in his debate. The rules we have are not his fancy opinions. The rules we have are the laws of this country and the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. That, Mr. Speaker, brings me to the other point which I wanted to make.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs read a letter that I sent while I was Solicitor General, which I was pleased to hear and which I endorse. I reminded the House that we must be vigilant to oppose and stamp out violence, terrorism, or unlawful means, even if the target is outside of Canada. If we allow terrorist activities to be planned in our country, to be practised in our country, to be financed and provisioned from our country, we risk bringing terrorism to Canada and increase the threat to innocent people around the world of being killed and injured. We have a policy in that area, a policy of opposing the use of violence. When a group espouses violence we should oppose the whole group.
The Secretary of State referred to the case of the FLQ. He tried to suggest that somehow or other that was like the three groups about which I am going to speak in a minute. The FLQ was a secret association dedicated, by its constitution and its common bond, to the violent overthrow of the established government in the Province of Quebec and in Canada. It participated officially in secret meetings, bombings and dynamiting. The Minister tried to draw an analogy between that and these three organizations, a meeting of one of which I and some of my colleagues attended. Wives, spouses, and children were present and it was a far cry from anything which could be called a terrorist organization.
On March 16, 1987, the Secretary of State for External Affairs wrote another letter warning Canadians about another group in the Sikh community called the Federation of Sikh Societies in Canada. What happened to them? I am not suggesting that he should have targeted that group, but why was the menu last year the Federation of Sikh Societies in Canada when this year the menu is three other Sikh groups in Canada? What is the Minister trying to tell us? What kind of consistency is coming from the Government? How can the Minister call a group a terrorist group on the basis that, as is indicated in the letter, although it is hard to believe, "some of their members have promoted or engaged in acts of violence"?
I want to pick a group which is beyond criticism to use as an example. Take the Roman Catholic Church and look at what some of its members are doing in Northern Ireland. They are terrorists. What does that tell you? Does that tell you that the Roman Catholic Church is a terrorist organization? Does that mean that Ministers of the Crown, Members of Parliament, and provincial premiers should stay away from Catholic organizations because some of their members are dedicated to the violent overthrow of the Government of Northern Ireland, the British Government, and to the establishment of an independent state there or an annexation or whatever? That is ridiculous. Yet that is exactly what he has done in this case.

March 10, 1988

The fact that he designated three groups, without adding the one group from last year, shows how mischievous this type of approach is. It has been alleged that some of the members of these groups have engaged in violence. For my purposes, I will not contest that, but what I am contesting is drawing a generalization about the group as a whole from the activities of a few members.
It would be different if these were terrorist groups. If the Minister or the Solicitor General were telling us that these were terrorist groups, he would even be fulfilling a duty because we should be warned by the Government of Canada about these matters. The Government has the powerful instruments of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service and the RCMP to learn about these activities which happen in Canadian society. It would be doing a service to Members of Parliament and provincial Premiers to warn us off from groups like that.
However, it is going too far for a Minister to draw a conclusion, from alleged facts that some members have engaged in or promoted terrorist activities, that the whole group is contaminated, irrespective of its goals, its membership and modus operandi.
My colleague, the Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), already stated that there are 20,000 Sikhs in one of these three organizations. It is an atrocious slur against a group of 20,000 people to say we should stay away from their meetings because some of their members-one, two or ten of the 20,000-have promoted or were engaged in terrorist activities.
The Government has betrayed us on multiculturalism. It has betrayed us on the proper approach to take in the face of separatism in other countries around the world. I hope this debate will lead the Government back to a more sensible, restrained and appropriate approach for a country like Canada toward the communities that live here and want to live freely and make all their views and values known in a law abiding manner, respectful of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SIKH ORGANIZATIONS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I listened carefully to what the Hon. Member said and tried to grasp the full meaning of his remarks. Setting aside the whole issue of terrorism, he spent a good deal of his time dealing with what he believes is a legitimate role for Canada, that is, to use Canada as a base of operations to promote separatism in other countries as long as it is peaceful dissent, as I understand him, in a land of free speech.
Will he enlarge on his concept of franchise operations in Canada from around the world who would feel free to use Canada as a base to promote separatism in other countries?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SIKH ORGANIZATIONS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not sure if "franchise operations" is a term of art. Unless it has some special meaning, I have no objection to that.
Let us take any particular ethnic community in Canada, including mine, for example. I am a member of the Jewish community. I am a Zionist. As a member of the Jewish community and as a Zionist, I have a view of how events in the Middle East should unfold. I am interested in it, I make financial contributions to it. I attend meetings on that subject and talk about how I feel that portion of the world should resolve its problems. Surely I am free to do that in this country.
I have Armenian friends and recently attended an important meeting at the Armenian Hall. They have ideas and expressed their views about what Turkey should do in relation to a very troubled province in their country.
The Government of Canada could be interested when manipulation of these groups occurs. Occasionally, foreign governments and international organizations may try to stage-manage the way in which a group would conduct itself. They may conduct various activities in an attempt to undermine some of the leaders of the community, for example, or in some way undermine the authenticity of the program of that community group. When that happens I think there is a role for the Government of Canada.
For example, when I was Solicitor General I learned how a community that was advocating independence in one part of the world was infiltrated by a foreign government opposed to that type of independence. There is a role for the Government to play in that circumstance. However, the Secretary of State has made statements about a group with 20,000 people, the World Sikh Organization, whose objectives as stated in its charter are, "To strive through peaceful means for the establishment of a Sikh nation Khalistan-", I am not suggesting that the Government or the RCMP must take that at face value. Perhaps a group will put in writing that it wants to use peaceful means in order to disguise the fact they are a terrorist organization. In this case, I do not believe that they are, nor does this group. The Government is not saying they are a terrorist organization, it is simply referring to some members out of that 20,000.
I am pleased to have this question because I want Government Members to at least see what it is they are rejecting. They are rejecting the idea that an ethnic community ought to be able to advocate what I call change in a certain part of the world. I have named a dozen areas where Canadians from those areas want change. I think the Government should not take sides officially, but certainly should not try to deter the groups by keeping other Canadians away from them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SIKH ORGANIZATIONS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are Tamils living in Canada who are concerned about the situation in Sri Lanka. There are Spanish people living in Canada who are concerned about the Basque and an area in France. There are Irish people concerned about what is happening in Northern Ireland. There are probably very few countries in the world today that do not have some group advocating separatism.
March 10, 1988

Toronto is a place where many immigrants and refugees have found a home but who still have legitimate domestic ties to their homeland. EIow many countries would the Elon. Member estimate should be encouraged, in one way or other, to carry on this kind of activity in Canada that would encourage separatism in another country? How many countries in the world can be represented in our country, which is then used as a base of operations to carry on strategic goals in another country?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SIKH ORGANIZATIONS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the Hon. Member, in asking that question, has a number in mind? I can only say that as long as these are authentic feelings being expressed by ethnic communities, the number will be the bottom line after freedom of expression is recognized for all the groups that care to express themselves.
I think it is also worth noting that there may be many other groups in the country or members of the community who feel that the country should stay together. A great many people who have come from India and Canada feel that India should stay together and remain one country. They have other ways of solving the grievances that are being put forward by the World Sikh Organization. Maybe there are even Sikhs-and I know there are-who feel that that country should stay together.
Is the Hon. Member suggesting that somehow or other the Government should take their side, that it should support that organization, that Members of Parliament and provincial Premiers attend their meetings while they boycott the meetings of the other side? Just to put the proposition is to show how ridiculous it is and how the position of the Government of Canada on this subject has not been thought out. Leave it to them, provided that they are bound by the fundamental code that they obey the laws of our country and respect the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. If we cannot say that they do not, then they have to be recognized as being allowed to do that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-SIKH ORGANIZATIONS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) has understandably been very critical of the policy of the federal Government as expressed in the letter from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in the debate arising from the motion of the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi). This motion states that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) urged upon the provincial Premiers a political boycott of three Sikh organizations in Canada. This potentially inflammatory interpretation of the Minister's remarks is an injustice to both the intent and the substance of his message which was to caution provincial Premiers who might be "drawn inadvertently" into activities associating them with individuals who condone acts of violence as a means of achieving political ends.

March 10, 1988
Supply
I wish to stress the word "individuals". It is of course evident to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and to all Hon. Members that the Government condemns the violent actions of certain individuals within a community, and not the community as a whole. Under no circumstances are we prepared to accept the notion that threats or actions endangering the life or well-being of any Canadian citizen, or any other person, are justified.
This Government embraces the belief that all Canadian citizens of every origin, including the Sikh community, many of whom live and worship in my riding of Lachine, have the constitutional freedom to be full and equal partners in the political, social, cultural and economic life of Canada. This nation was founded on that belief.
From the time of its first occupation by our aboriginal peoples to the arrival of British and French settlers and then immigrants from Europe and all parts of the world this country has been defined by a diversity of cultures, traditions and beliefs. It has promised certain freedoms to all those who choose to live here. As Canada grew and became a nation the ideal of a truly free country in which the rights of all its citizens are respected and protected grew with it.
Writing in 1865, Sir Hector Langevin, who became Canada's first Secretary of State, declared the principle, "Justice to all races, to all regions, to all nationalities and to all interests". That principle not only became a primary feature of government policy and legislation in the years to come, it became one of the fundamental values of our society as well.
On August 4, 1960, the values of equality of opportunity and participation for all members of our society were upheld by law when the Canadian Bill of Rights was approved by the House of Commons and signed by that great parliamentarian and Prime Minister of the day, John G. Diefenbaker. The Bill affirmed privileges to which all Canadians are entitled. It states:
In Canada there have existed and shall continue to exist without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex ... human rights
and fundamental freedoms.
Again, in 1982, the Bill's guarantee of human rights was greatly strengthened with the proclamation of a new Constitution Act which contained the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. In both spirit and wording the Charter provides the guidance through which this Government seeks to ensure the full and equal partnership of all Canadians in the life of their country. It also clearly states the rights and responsibilities of all citizens. I want to remind Hon. Members of some of the Charter's basic commitments.
Article 15 affirms equality rights for every individual. Article 25 recognizes aboriginal rights. Article 27 is an affirmation of the multicultural heritage of Canadians.
After the current Government took office in September, 1984, it initiated a review of existing multiculturalism policy and programs with the aim of developing a new policy based
on the realities of today and the expectations of tomorrow. But even while this review was under way the Government was taking significant steps to reinforce multiculturalism as a cornerstone of Canadian life.
They include establishing the House of Commons Standing Committee on Multiculturalism; convening the first national conference on policing in urban multicultural societies held in Vancouver in 1984, and continued collaboration on a national strategy on police-minority relations; holding the first federal-provincial-territorial conference of Ministers responsible for multiculturalism in Winnipeg in 1985; and introducing the Employment Equity Act of 1986, which required federally-regulated employers to provide improved access to employment opportunities for women and the disabled, as well as for aboriginal peoples and racial minorities.
Also included is the launching of a program within federal Departments and agencies to ensure the hiring and promotion of members of racial minorities; increasing the rate of appointments of qualified members of Canadian cultural communities to federal boards and commissions in order that they better reflect the cultural diversity of Canada; and finally, proclaiming Canada's participation in the second decade for action to combat racism and racial discrimination. In regard to this latter initiative, the Department of the Secretary of State has a mandate for implementing Canada's international human rights obligations. It carries out that mandate in cooperation with various federal and provincial authorities.
The Department co-ordinates Canada's federal-provincial monitoring of how we are complying with measures guaranteeing the rights contained in the United Nations international convenant on civil and political rights, and the international convenant on economic and social rights, as well as certain other human rights treaties.
Through the Department of the Secretary of State the Government focuses on promoting human rights throughout the population at large. It is concerned with creating a wide-ranging awareness of understanding of basic human rights and freedoms. It concerns itself with the voluntary sector, with community-based projects that safeguard human rights, with public education and curriculum materials promoting knowledge of human rights. At the same time, the Department is concerned with enshrining justice in law.
In fact, the preamble to the Canadian multiculturalism Act, Bill C-93, tabled in this House on December 1, invokes the minority and racial rights provisions of the international convenant on civil and political rights, and the international convention on the elimination of all forms of racial discrimination.
The proposed multiculturalism Act is an historic piece of legislation which will be debated fully in this House next week. I wish to remind Hon. Members of some of its highlights and its provisions to ensure the preservation of cultural heritage of
March 10, 1988

all Canadians of every origin, to promote the full participation of all Canadians in our society, and to enhance harmonious race relations and cross-cultural understanding.
The multiculturalism Act acknowledges the vital contribution to Canada of all its cultural and racial communities. It lays out the framework in which everyone will be able to participate in the business of the nation on a basis of complete equality. The supremacy of human rights is the essence of equality.
Far from boycotting any of Canada's racial communities, this Government seeks to affirm in law that all Canadian citizens are full and equal partners in our society. It seeks to recognize multiculturalism as a central feature of our society, not only for today but for the 21st century and beyond.
As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) clearly stated:
Multiculturalism is an affirmation of our commitment that Canadians of all ethnic and racial backgrounds have the right to equal recognition and equal opportunity in this country. Thus multiculturalism lies at the very heart of the idea of Canada, of our sense of country... It reflects where we have come from and where we are going.
The Canadian multiculturalism Bill sets forth the multiculturalism policy of Canada and it entrenches in law a government-wide commitment to implement that policy. It states that the federal Government will provide leadership to Canadian institutions and people to reinforce an appreciation and understanding of multiculturalism throughout the country.
The Bill sets out a clear mandate for the Minister responsible for multiculturalism. In particular, it assigns to the Minister the responsibility to encourage and promote a coordinated approach to multiculturalism throughout the federal Government. The Bill provides in legislation a clear and direct process of accountability through the tabling of an annual report to Parliament on the implementation of the multiculturalism policy of Canada, and the review of this report on a permanent basis by a parliamentary committee.
When passed, the multiculturalism Bill will not only preserve the diverse heritage of this country's identity, it will provide a means of improving intercultural relationships in the present. The Bill provides a legislative base for programs that will assist cultural preservation, combat discrimination, and promote institutional change.
For many years the Government has supported programs which preserve and promote multiculturalism and which work to protect human rights in Canada. But the proposed Act gives legal substance to those programs. It underlines the commitment of the Government of Canada to help to create a fair and tolerant society for all Canadians in which the principles of equality, diversity, and community are an overriding characteristic.
The Government has reason to be proud of its record. It is a Government that refuses to accept discrimination, intolerance
Supply
or bigotry against any racial or cultural community or individual member of that community.
It has been proven again and again that Canada's unique multicultural character helps to give this country a healthy and dynamic social life, cultural life, and business life. Our diversity is one of our greatest national assets. It has brought us enormous economic benefits and increasing international respect.
We have shown the world that we are a nation committed to fairness, equality, and freedom. That conviction may be our most valuable natural resource, and one that we can be proud to export to the world.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 82-SIKH ORGANIZATIONS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate on this very fundamental question of human rights, a question which really goes to the core of Canada as a multicultural nation.
Canadians across the land were shocked when they learned of the attempt by the Conservative Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to dictate to elected officials at the provincial level, and presumably to officials at the local level and even officials in his own caucus, which organizations they could meet with in Canada.
March 10, 1988

Let us clear up the confusion right now. The Hon. Member for Lachine (Mr. Layton) who spoke just a few minutes ago suggested that the Minister was simply saying that there may be certain functions which might be inappropriate to be attended. That is simply not the case.
The letter-and I have a copy of it before me-sent by the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the Premiers states that the majority of invitations received from the Canadian Sikh community indeed can be accepted and would be valuable, but it goes on to say:
There are, however, three Sikh organizations which exist largely to advocate the creation of an independent Sikh state, known as "Khalistan". These... organizations are the Babbar Khalsa, the International Sikh Youth Federation ... and the World Sikh Organization.
The letter goes on to suggest:
Some members of these organizations have also engaged in or promote violent activities aimed at Indian interests in Canada or elsewhere. The activities of these organizations have been a significant irritant in our relations with India. The government of India has taken particular exception when elected officials attend functions sponsored by these organizations.
Who is it that is running the foreign affairs policy of Canada? Is it the Secretary of State for External Affairs of Canada, or is it the Government of India?
When we examine the response of our Secretary of State for External Affairs, it seems that in fact our policy in respect of this very important question is not being dictated by Canadians, by Canadian interests, but rather is a policy which is being dictated by the Government of India itself. I take exception to that suggestion, and I believe that many Canadians take exception to it.
The letter goes on to indicate that the Secretary of State for External Affairs believes that elected officials should avoid "events and activities which could be perceived as supporting the Sikh organizations mentioned above or their objective in the creation of an independent Sikh state".
Many of us thought that we had a Charter of Rights and Freedoms which respected freedom of speech, which respected freedom of association, and which respected the multicultural heritage of Canadians. However, this kind of insulting, degrading attack on a community which has contributed an enormous amount to Canada is fundamentally unacceptable.
I would have hoped that the Secretary of State for External Affairs would have recognized that, would have stood in his place and said: "I am sorry, upon reflection I realize that I was tarnishing an entire community", a community of some
200,000	Canadians who have contributed an enormous amount to our society, I might say, in the face of considerable adversity over the years.
It was early in this century, just after the turn of the century, that the first Sikhs came to Canada, to my own Province of British Columbia, to work in the forest industry. From the very beginning the Sikh community in Canada was the subject of government-sponsored, government initiated racist policies. The vote was denied to them, even though they
Supply
were all British subjects and other British subjects were entitled to the vote. They were forbidden to bring their wives and their families to join them. They were forbidden to own any timber-cutting rights or to hold any public office.
In an incident that we remember particularly vividly in British Columbia in 1914, some 376 would-be Sikh immigrants were kept stranded aboard a freighter, the Kamagata Maru, for some two months without water, without food, and were finally turned around and sent back to Asia, leaving the local community in turmoil. That long history of racism is one which we should recognize and take steps to overcome.
Evidently we have seen other disturbing illustrations of unfair attacks on the Sikh community in Canada. CSIS, the civilian security intelligence service, and indeed the RCMP, in their response to certain violent incidents, have effectively branded an entire community as being unlawful or as supporting terrorism. Members of the Sikh community are law-abiding, upright, outstanding Canadians who have contributed a great deal to Canadian society. That community itself is the first to denounce violence and acts of terrorism. It is for that reason that the community has taken such strong exception to some of the actions of CSIS and the RCMP in recent months.
I have been privileged to attend a number of functions at Sikh temples in the lower mainland of British Columbia at the Khalsa Diwan temple, the Akali Singh Sikh and others. I have spoken at various public meetings. In attendance at those public meetings have been representatives of organizations which the Secretary of State for External Affairs has singled out. I make no apology for that, Mr. Speaker. I was proud to have been invited to participate in those functions and proud to be invited to speak to Canadians who have contributed a great deal. Many of my constituents are from the Sikh community in Burnaby. Indeed, there are 60,000 Sikhs in British Columbia out of a population in Canada of some 200,000. It is precisely because of the strong history of respect for the law that this kind of attack on these three organizations is so unacceptable.
I noted in the letter from the Secretary of State for External Affairs that the Government of India has taken particular exception when elected officials attend functions sponsored by these organizations. There are some who are concerned. I have heard a number of representatives at the Sikh community voice this concern that, indeed, agents of the Indian security service may, in fact, be participating in actions here in Canada to undermine the credibility and respect of the Sikh community. We know that the Canadian Government sent back to India rather quickly certain people who supposedly were diplomats working out of the consulate, I believe, in Toronto. I want to flag this as one area of concern that Canada not in any way permit agents of the Indian security service to work on Canadian soil, whether they be acting as agents provocateurs or in any other capacity whatsoever.

March 10, 1988
Supply
The implications of this letter written by the Secretary of State for External Affairs are deeply troubling. If this very dangerous policy is applied in other sectors of Canadian society, where will it stop?
I recently returned from a visit to the Middle East. While there I visited the occupied West Bank, and Gaza, Israel. I met with Palestinians who are part of a national tragedy whose plight has been ignored for far too long by the community of nations, Palestinians who are seeking the right to selfdetermination, the right to decide for themselves on their own future, to decide who will represent them in international forums and ultimately to have the right of statehood accepted. Is it, in fact, the policy of the Government of Canada that Palestinian organizations in Canada that advocate an independent state for the Palestinians should be boycotted by elected representatives? That would be deeply offensive and would be an unwarranted interference in the lives of those particular organizations.
The implication of what the Secretary of State for External Affairs is doing is very dangerous. He is cutting off the channels of communication through various organizations, the World Sikh Organization, the Babbar Khalsa and the International Sikh Youth Federation. One can only imagine who else is on the list. He is cutting off communication with these organizations, which are certainly advocating a number of important policies but which are advocating them in a peaceful and open way. If these organizations are being told that they cannot communicate with other Canadians, that they cannot communicate with elected representatives then, in effect, the Secretary of State for External Affairs is encouraging the very kinds of acts that he purports to be opposed to. That is the danger of this approach.
It is through these organizations that the Sikh community in Canada can communicate its concerns to elected representatives. If then the organizations are treated as persona non grata, if they are driven underground and dealt with as if they do not exist, then as sure as I am standing here other organizations will surface which say, "If the Government of Canada will not speak to our elected representatives then we will take action". That action may be precisely what the Secretary of State for External Affairs indicates he wants to avoid. I suggest that, from that perspective alone, this policy is not only insulting but is counterproductive.
Where do we go from here, Mr. Speaker? I would suggest that this matter must not be allowed to rest with a one day debate in the House of Commons. I would suggest rather, as my colleague the House Leader for the New Democratic Party has proposed during his very thoughtful remarks earlier today, that either a special parliamentary committee be struck or that a standing committee be given a mandate to inquire into the implications of this matter from the perspective of human rights, of the multiculturalism policy in Canada, and, most important, of the implications for a proud and law abiding community of Sikhs in Canada that has been tarnished and insulted by the actions of this Minister.
I was disappointed that the Premier of Ontario in responding to the letter of the Secretary of State for External Affairs chose to indicate that the Liberal Government in Ontario would respect that decision. I quote from a story in The Globe and Mail, a respected national newspaper, for February 26, which reads:
Ontario Premier David Peterson promised yesterday to obey Mr. Clark's
request. "We will take it seriously", he told reporters outside his office.
"Obviously we don't want to cause some kind of international incident or
something embarrassing to the Minister of External Affairs".
If the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) wants to get up and disagree with the Premier of Ontario, certainly that is his right to do so.

I think it is important and it is regrettable that the Liberal Premier of Ontario apparently has jumped into bed with the Tory Secretary of State for External Affairs in a way that does no credit whatsoever to the Sikh community in Canada. I would urge the Government to reconsider and recognize that a mistake has been made, not just a mistake that can be remedied by the Secretary of State for External Affairs standing up saying Canadians are free to attend whichever organizations they want, but one that can be remedied by the Secretary of State for External Affairs standing in his place in the House saying, "I was wrong, Mr. Speaker. I made a mistake. I tarnished and insulted the Sikh community in Canada unfairly. I recognize that and I want to apologize to that community".
That would be the honourable and noble thing to do. That is what we hoped the Secretary of State for External Affairs might have done today. In the absence of that, we are left with the alternative of proceeding to a parliamentary committee. Certainly we in the New Democratic Party intend to take this matter up in the appropriate parliamentary committee. It should not be left to the Sikh community to sue for libel. It has been suggested that there may be a lawsuit. Lawsuits cost money. When the community has been attacked, why should it have to spend resources to defend itself? Surely that is the role of the Government. The role of the Government is to stand up for the multicultural traditions of Canada and not to attack a community that has contributed an enormous amount to Canadian society.
I support the motion and I join with my colleagues in condemning this attack on the Sikh community of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it is perhaps fortuitous that I have a chance to enter the debate at this moment. The Hon. Member will know that I am a person who speaks the truth. I heard his colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), say on more than one occasion that the Liberals were barking up the wrong tree, that we were trying to score cheap political points and we should not ask questions on this issue. He shouted those remarks from his seat. I heard them quite distinctly. He said the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) was right. I suspect that is why the NDP has not asked any questions on this issue in the House.
However, I am happy the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) is here. I hope he can get his colleague on the right track and that he will lead the charge with questions in the House. He can join with some Members on the government side who have displayed courage in standing up to the Minister. He is a very powerful Minister in the Government, and even some Conservative Members stood up and questioned his wisdom in this letter and its slur on the Sikh community.
I welcome the participation of the NDP in this debate. I am glad they have finally seen the light. I can only say, thank God for Members like the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) who continued to pursue this issue in the House. Thank God for Members like the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner) as well. If they had not continued to pursue the issue in the House, I dare say we would not be having this debate today, which debate I think is very important to the fundamental principles of democracy in this country.
In his letter the Minister points out a number of reasons why he claims that we as Members of Parliament should not attend functions of the International Sikh Youth Federation, the World Sikh Organization, or the Babbar Khalsa. One reason is that these organizations exist largely to advocate the creation of an independent Sikh state known as "Khalisthn". I suggest that if Members of Parliament follow that advice and refuse to attend functions of any organization that wishes to dissociate itself from a Government under whose umbrella it is currently found, we would not be allowed to attend Ukrainian functions or functions of many eastern bloc countries including Lithuania. We would not be allowed to attend functions of organizations promoting the freedom of the people of Afghanistan. This weekend I am going to be attending a function in my riding dealing with a small community in eastern Europe known as the Slovaks. If I took the words of the Minister to heart and substituted the word "Slovak" for the word "Sikh", then I should not go to that function. They would like to see the creation of an independeht Slovak state. The same thing applies to Ukrainian Freedom Fighters and the Canadian Polish Congress.
March 10, 1988

There are many nations around the world fighting for an independent cultural and political identity. Are we as Canadians then to say that we will attend no functions organized by the Tamil community? I dare say that Members of Parliament not only have a responsibility but a right to attend cultural functions of people in our communities who represent various political points of view. They may represent viewpoints which differ from that of their respective Governments. That is why we live in a democracy. That is why Canada is the greatest country on earth. People come to this country and they have an opportunity, if they disagree with the Government of their homeland, to form an organization to that effect.
The Parti Quebecois had as one of its founding principles the separation of Quebec from Canada. They exercised their democratic right to express their point of view and they represented the majority in certain legislatures at certain times in our history. I did not agree with them or that principle, but I defended to the utmost their right to express those views in a free and democratic society.
If you listen to the remarks of the Minister in the House in responding to the questions of the Hon. Member, he keeps going back to the fact that these organizations exist largely because they support a political viewpoint different from that of the Government of India. Frankly that is no answer at all. That response eliminates any involvement by Canadian politicians with Ukrainian Freedom Fighters, the Canadian Polish Congress, or dozens of other Canadian-based organizations which exist in whole or in part to promote freedom from enslavement in their own countries. That is the kind of expression of support for freedom that we as Canadians support and want to foster.
That is one part of the Minister's letter which is absolutely and totally false and groundless. Let us get to the second part which deals with his contention that:
Some members of these organizations have also engaged in or promote
violent activities-
The Roman Catholic Church is a very large organization in Canada. I happen to be a member of that church. Does that mean that if another Roman Catholic is caught robbing a bank or in some way breaking the law of the land, somehow all members of the Roman Catholic Church are now persona non grata? If you apply the logic, or the lack of logic, of the Minister in this letter, that is the position all Canadians must take. If any person in any organization is involved in any criminal activity, then de facto, Members of Parliament are supposed to refuse to associate with other members of that organization.
Does the Minister not realize that this kind of slanderous accusation against the whole community is a blight on what we respect and know as democracy? Surely there is not a Canadian, whether of Sikh, Ukrainian or other origin, who would not want to see terrorism in this and other countries stamped out, terrorism of any stripe by any organization. However, the Minister does not cite individuals in his letter. No individual

charges have been laid. If they are, then let them be dealt with in a court of law. What he is doing is appealing to the lowest common denominator. He is appealing to a sense of racism which says that this organization will be blackballed by all Canadians because the Minister claims some members are involved in so-called violent activities.
The Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata) put it best when he said that if people are involved in violent activities, whether they be members of these organizations, the Canadian Legion, or whatever, we must seek them out, lay charges, and prosecute them in a court of law. That is why we have a justice system. The system is not such that the Minister, who is supposed to represent the interests of Canada, can issue a letter which, in one fell swoop, discredits the hard work of a whole community and the thousands of Canadians of Sikh origin who are working hard to build lives for themselves and their children in Canada and have the right to belong to cultural and social organizations which give them some link with their past and the futures of their families and their own cultural heritage. I do not think we deny that right.
I will speak next April at a rally to be held by the Armenian community in this country. We do not want to see the day when the Secretary of State for External Affairs will write a letter saying that someone has been involved in something. Armenians have been subject to that kind of blasphemy, not by the Secretary of State for External Affairs but by allegations that an individual was involved in a terrorist act. Yes, Mr. Speaker, individuals in every community will, from time to time, break the law. They will, in a misguided way, decide to take out their frustrations in a violent fashion. They should be prosecuted with the full force of the law of this country.
However, we do not want to create a system similar in many respects to what many of these people have left behind. We do not want to create a system where, by virtue of sanction of the Government of Canada, we are blackballing a whole people, a whole community, a whole culture, a whole racial group because of the activities of a few and, in this case, the unproven allegation of the activities of a few.
I cannot tell you, Mr. Speaker, how offensive I find the contents of this letter. The Secretary of State talked about Members of Parliament lending their good offices or stature to organizations by attending functions and supporting, or at least involving themselves in, the work of those organizations. What disturbs me most is that the Secretary of State does not realize that this letter, written in his capacity as the Secretary of State for External Affairs, is, in my opinion, a travesty of democracy. It should be the bane of every freedom-loving individual in this country. It should be rejected by every person who has chosen to come to Canada or been born in Canada because of the freedom which we have here. The Minister should realize that when he lends his name, his Department, and his reputation to the attack present in the allegations made in this letter he is discrediting the whole country of Canada.

As a country we have developed a certain reputation, sometimes warranted and sometimes not. Last night we saw a very sad story on the CBC with regard to our native community. Sometimes our record is not what we would like it to be. However, as a nation we have developed a worldwide reputation for tolerance, justice, and understanding. When Canadians go to Europe or other countries they receive a warm welcome as Canadians and this is very special for this country. We are the only country which, as a nation, has been awarded international recognition for our work in accepting refugees as a result of the involvement of church groups and individuals in the exodus of the boat people from Vietnam. We have a long and proud tradition, and the Minister does not realize that in one fell swoop, with a single letter, he can destroy that whole tradition.
No one is asking Members of Parliament to support the objectives of the World Sikh Organization. No one is asking Canadian Members of Parliament to say yea or nay, to say that they believe that there should be the creation of an independent Sikh state or that they believe that there should not. However, as Canadians and parliamentarians we owe our constituents the right to a climate within which to express their point of view. We should join them and point out the activities which we have seen, including the questionable activities of the police of the state of India with regard to search and seizure and the transfer of information between the RCMP in Canada and the police in India. We have a responsibility to ensure that the RCMP or CSIS is not aiding and abetting the persecution of the families of Canadian nationals back in their homeland as a result of the exchange of erroneous information.
We have a job to do. I have met on many occasions with representatives of the Sikh community in my riding. I have written to the Secretary of State for External Affairs to express my concern, and I consider that to be part of my responsibility. If I have the opportunity to support the work of freedom-loving people in all parts of the globe I consider it my responsibility to do so. Surely that is all that Members of Parliament ask from the Secretary of State for External Affairs. They do not ask for a blanket condemnation of an entire group of people based on the alleged actions of a few which, if proven, must be illegal and therefore must be dealt with properly in a court of law.

Mr. Speaker, within today's debate it is important in my view to stress this government's performance in the area of human rights.
As you know, the Secretary of State is responsible for co-ordinating human rights in Canada. In that capacity, he works with his Cabinet colleagues and the provincial ministers responsible for human rights to ensure the fulfilment of our national and internationl commitments in that area.
Promoting human rights is not the specific responsibility of any one level of Government or interest group. It is of basic importance to all human beings on the planet. We should all be concerned with promoting better public awareness and understanding of human rights matters. Awareness helps preserve those rights we fought at home and abroad to protect an improve upon. Canada is party to a number of international agreements dealing with human rights, including the International Covenant-Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, the International Covenant on Civic and Political Rights, the International Convention on the Elimination of all Forms of Racial Discrimination, the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, the Convention against Torture and other Cruel, Inhumane and Degrading Penalties or Treatments.
Co-operation with the United Nations, Canada is taking an active part in the implementation of special projects, including the Decade for Action to Combat Racism and the Racial Discrimination and the Decade on the Handicapped. Those are programs extending over 10 years and promoting public awareness of those specific problems.
In that respect, during the coming Federal-Provincial-Territorial Conference of ministers in charge of human rights, that will be chaired by the Secretary of State, participants will have an opportunity to discuss the second Decade for Action to Combat Racism and Racial Discrimination.
As you can see, Ministers and officials responsible for human rights within federal, provincial and territorial administrations meet regularly to consider issues raised by the implementation of international treaties related to human rights and, more generally, to keep abreast of new developments in that field.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote brief passages from some of the instruments and covenants to which Canada is a signatory, just so you may fully appreciate the scope of our country's commitments.
First, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights provides that nations, and I quote:
-shall strive by teaching and education to promote respect for these rights
and freedoms and by progressive measures, national and international, to
secure their universal and effective recognition and observance-
Canada also ratified the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. Here is article 13(1):
Supply
Member States recognize the right of everyone to education. They agree
that education shall be directed to the development of the human personality
and sense of dignity, and to the strengthening of respect for human rights and
fundamental freedoms.
Canada simply cannot take such commitments lightly. We are expected to report to international organizations on progress we make in honouring our commitments.
We discharge this obligation through reports drafted in close co-operation with the provinces and territories, as well as with federal ministries and organizations responsible for implementing various measures specified in treaties.
In 1986-87, the Human Rights Directorate of the Department of the Secretary of State contributed substantially to Canada's delegations when the United Nations was examining the report on Sections 13 to 15 of the International Convenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, in April 1986, in New York, and also when the United States was studying Canada's Seventh and Eighth Report concerning the Convention on the Elimination of all Forms of Racial Discrimination, in Geneva in March 1987.
Mr. Speaker, the reports were well received. Canada was commended by the United Nations for taking its international obligations very seriously and for the quality and depth of its reports.
Perhaps I may take as an example a passage from the report tabled by the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination during the forty-second session of the UN General Assembly in 1987.
The reports were presented by Canada's representative, who referred to various constitutional and legislative mechanisms that for ensuring respect for human rights, including the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms as incorporated in the Canadian Constitution Act, 1982, the Canadian Criminal Code and the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms.
He emphasized the leading role played by Canada, more specifically within the Commonwealth, in the fight against apartheid as well as his Government's commitment to continue to put pressure on the South African Government to abolish this system. He informed members of the Committee of measures taken by the federal Government and the provincial and territorial governments to achieve the objectives of the second decade of the fight against racism and racial discrimination, and he mentioned the Special Committee on Visible Minorities created by the Parliament of Canada as well as special measures to promote and protect vulnerable groups with respect to employment and training.
New legislation had been passed concerning employment equity, which obliged federally regulated employers to establish action plans guaranteeing equality in the workplace for visible minorities, women, the disabled and native people. In the case of the latter, Canada's representative informed the
