Committee that important initiatives had been taken for their benefit.
Committee members stressed the quality of the reports submitted and commended the Canadian Government for its efforts in implementing the Convention and recognizing the ethnic character of a multicultural society.
The mass of information they contained deserved the attention of all other nations party to the Convention. Those reports could be taken as models by all federal states where the responsibility for human rights is shared between the Federation and its component parts.
You will probably agree with me, Mr. Speaker, that it is quite encouraging to receive such praise from the United Nations on the implementation of human rights in Canada.
Canada has a lot to offer to the international community. In that respect, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) announced in December 1987 the government's intention to establish an international co-operation center for the promotion of human rights and the development and strengthening of democratic institutions. That new Crown corporation will be called the International Centre for Human Rights and Democratic Development. It will deal first and foremost with co-operation between Canada and developing nations, and will be funded as such under Official Development Assistance. Eventually, the new centre may call upon other public and private sources to enter, if it so wishes into cooperation with developed countries.
The establishment of such an institution was first proposed in 1986 by the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Commons on Canada's external relations, and accepted in principle by this Government in December of the same year.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs announced a month ago the appointment of two eminent Canadians, Professor Gisele Cote-Harper and Mr. John Courtney, to undertake a series of consultations across the country with non-governmental organizations, labour unions, religious groups and interested individuals. Those consultations are aimed at obtaining views and suggestions on the establishment of such an institution and on the ways and means of promoting co-operation with Third World Countries in the area of human rights and democratic development.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) took every opportunity during their journeys through foreign lands to state clearly what we think of human rights violations. The Secretary of State for External Affairs pleaded directly with Messrs. Gromyko and Shevardnadze, here and in the Soviet Union, to secure the release of political and other prisoners.
In recognition of his efforts, Mr. Speaker, last November the Association of Canadian Lawyers and Jurists for Soviet Jewry presented him with its annual human rights award.
During his recent visit to Zimbabwe and Senegal the Prime Minister met with six heads of African governments, including the President of the Front Line States and the former President of the Organization of African Unity.
In his discussions with the African leaders, reference was often made to the rapidly deteriorating situation in South Africa and its impact on neighbouring nations. Considering that the problem may not be solved through negotiations, the Prime Minister again set forth Canada's position as he had explained it in his October 1985 address to the United Nations, namely that existing sanctions will indeed be maintained.
The Prime Minister made it quite clear that Canada would bring pressure to bear in support of those who seek to restore justice in South Africa. As you may recall, Mr. Speaker, it was in December 1986 that the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees presented the Governor General with the Nansen medal. The decoration was not meant for a Canadian citizen in particular but for the entire Canadian people as acknowledgement of their essential and lasting contribution to the refugee cause.
I might point out that it was the first time the medal, created in 1954, was awarded to a country. We can all stand proud.
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful for this opportunity to highlight some of the achievements of our Government and to tell the Canadian people that their Government's performance in the realm of human rights is second to none.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to make a few comments on the motion of the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi). I think that he has moved a very good and valuable motion, and I would like to read it into the record one more time. It states:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Secretary of State for External Affairs erred seriously in urging upon the Provincial Premiers a political boycott of three Sikh organizations in Canada, thereby condemning entire groups on the basis of unsubstantiated allegations against individuals and, consequently undermining the multicultural fabric of Canadian society;
That this House, while condemning violence and terrorism as political instruments, affirms that all Canadian citizens, regardless of origin must not be subjected to any coercion, intimidation or other action by the Government designed to prevent their free and peaceful expression of their opinions and concerns about events and issues in Canada or in other lands; and
That this House therefore demands that the Government provide Parliament with all relevant information that led to its aforementioned communication with the Provinces and provide the Canadian Sikh community with a full, public opportunity to defend its honour and integrity and that the Government immediately withdraw its allegations and issue a full apology to
March 10, 1988

all Canadians, and to the Canadian Sikh community in particular, for initiating an unprovoked attack on the rights and freedoms of Canadian citizens and for thereby subverting federal multiculturalism policy.
The reason for the Hon. Member's motion is the letter that was sent last December by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to seven provincial Premiers. In that letter he states:
There are, however, three Sikh organizations which exist largely to advocate the creation of an independent Sikh state, known as "Khalistan". These three organizations are the Babbar Khalsa, the International Sikh Youth Federation, and the World Sikh Organization. Some members of these organizations have also engaged in or promote violent activities aimed at Indian interests in Canada and elsewhere. The activities of these organizations have been a significant irritant in our relations with India. The government of India has taken particular exception when elected officials attend functions sponsored by these organizations.
Later on in the letter he states:
-I would appreciate your cooperation in avoiding events and activities which could be perceived as supporting the Sikh organizations mentioned above or their objective in the creation of an independent Sikh state.
When we consider the fact that this letter was sent secretly to seven Premiers we have to ask some very serious questions about what the Government is trying to do in terms of its relationship to the multicultural community in Canada, in particular its relationship to the Sikh community. What we are dealing with is a secret memo, a memo that would have the effect of subverting the access that members of the Sikh community would have to elected provincial officials.
They would not know what had happened to them. It was as though a whispering campaign had taken place saying that such and such a person has some grave disease and no one should associate with him and yet no one would come out in the open to make any accusations. In effect, that is what the Government has done with the Sikh community and with these organizations. It is a silent denial of access. It is a whispering campaign.
I know that it is not considered good parliamentary form to mention the Secretary of State for External Affairs by name. However, I would like to point out that he seems to have taken his namesake rather too seriously. I refer to his name, Joe. He seems to be taking rather seriously his relationship with another Joe, Joe McCarthy, because this kind of tactic smacks of McCarthyism. It is the sort of tactic that Joe McCarthy would use. It is not worthy of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It is an attempt to smear an entire organization by association.
We could ask where it will all end. Different Hon. Members have asked that and have pointed out that Members attend meetings of Ukranian, Estonian, Latvian, and Lithuanian organizations. The Eritreans have been involved in a long-term struggle against Ethiopia for independence. There are Members of the House who meet with the Eritrean organizations, and I presume that there are Members who give funds to Eritrean relief.
Supply
Where will it all end? What will be considered to be beyond the pale as far as the Secretary of State for External Affairs is concerned?
We must recognize that all Members of Parliament, all public officials, be they provincial, municipal, or federal, must exercise some discretion when it comes to meeting with different organizations. However, to put some groups beyond the pale and to circulate a memo suggesting that elected officials should not meet with them raises very serious questions about the openness of our democracy.
A few weeks ago I attended a kind of ethnic organization dinner and was seated next to a person who spoke with a fairly heavy accent. He was advocating the dismemberment of a country with which we have very close relations. In fact, he was a Scottish nationalist and I was attending a Burns' dinner. He was advocating Scottish nationalism, the breaking up of the United Kingdom. We have very close relations with the United Kingdom. Many of us are members of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association. There I was sitting next to someone who was a Scottish nationalist. Perhaps that is beyond the pale as well. I see that Your Honour recognizes that that is a rather ludicrous situation, but I submit that what we have here is a ludicrous situation which has tragic implications for the Sikh community.
When we step back a little and look at what has happened, we realize that a people have been maligned unjustly. Sikhs form a very important cultural and religious community within my constituency, within my Province of British Columbia, and within Canada as a whole. They have a long history in the Cowichan Valley. They first arrived in the Cowichan Valley at the turn of the century and were very involved in the sawmilling industry. Because of the racist immigration policies of Canada at that time, there was a long period of time when they were not allowed to bring in their families. There was also a time when they were denied the vote, even though they were British subjects. They were not allowed to have timber licences. They were really confined in a ghetto or ghettoized, yet they continued to work and to add to the prosperity of British Columbia.
These early immigrants worked to build a union and fought for better conditions for all woodworkers in British Columbia. Since 1967, when the immigration laws were changed, more immigrant families have come to the area. I think that this has changed the whole perception of the Sikh community in the Cowichan Valley. They used to be forced to live as single males in bunk houses. Now we see them as family people, people concerned about their families, about their communities, about building their temples, and about maintaining their religious faith. Of course, being long established in the Cowichan Valley, they diversified. They are no longer simply involved in the woodworking industry. They are involved in business and in the professions as teachers, lawyers, and public sector workers.

March 10, 1988
Supply
Two years ago the first member of the Sikh community was elected to the Legislature of British Columbia. Mo Sihota, from the constituency of Esquimalt-Port Renfrew, which takes in part of my constituency, I am proud to say is a New Democrat. I am also proud to say that he is one of the most outstanding members of the British Columbia Legislature today, which is recognized by people right across the board. He is an outstanding member of the Legislature, coming from the Sikh community with its history.
It has been my privilege at different times to attend worship services in three of the Sikh temples in my constituency. It is worth-while reminding Canadians of some of the basic Sikh beliefs. They believe in one God. They believe in equality for all people. After every worship service there is a communal meal at which people share food. This is important in our world where food is not shared, where large numbers of people go hungry. It is important to have that sacramental sense of sharing food and tying it in with worship.
It is important to recognize the contributions of Sikhs to my particular area, to my province, and to Canada as a whole. Also it is important to emphasize the fact that they are family people. They are community people. They are hard working and they are thrifty.
As I said, recently we have had more immigrants from India, mainly from the Punjab, the traditional homeland of the Sikhs. I remember in the late 1970s, when I was first becoming involved in running for federal office, talking with the late Tommy Douglas who pointed out that most Sikhs in our area were supporters of the All-Indian Congress Party, the forerunner of the Congress I Party. This meant that at that time they were supporters of a united India. Many of them believed in a united India, which was part of the vision of Mahatma Gandhi. The Sikhs had worked with other Indians in support of that ideal.
However, there was the growth of a separatist movement in India, a movement for a separate state called Khalistan. Unfortunately, that movement has been tragically mishandled, and I think that there have been tragic mistakes made on both sides of the issue. We can say that, looking at the situation from the security and comfort of Canada. One tragedy seemed to lead to another. When, on the orders of Indira Gandhi, the troops stormed the sacred temple, the Golden Temple at Amritsar, 1,000 people were killed. That destroyed any sense of confidence of the people in the Congress I Party. The Sikhs were no longer able to have faith in that kind of situation. Then, when two Sikh bodyguards assassinated Indira Ganghi, the tragedy was compounded. To compound it even more, it unleashed a fury of violence, which resulted in the massacre of some 3,000 Sikhs in India, mostly in the capital of Delhi. The Government took no real action to protect them at that time.
Naturally it had an effect upon Canadian Sikhs, particularly upon more recent immigrants who still had relatives and friends back in India, and naturally this feeling was exploited by militants who looked to the establishment of Khalistan.
Certainly there have been some very well publicized instances of violence. There have been suggestions that perhaps some of those instances of violence were caused by agents provocateurs from the Indian Government. I do not know. There is sufficient doubt at least to place questions on the issue, and the Canadian Government has requested that some people be sent back to India from our consulates.
In my own riding, there was a police raid on the Sikh temple at Duncan, which was highly publicized. We had great difficulty in trying to get information as to what was behind the raid. Lor months and even years the police refused to release information. Here we have this letter from the Secretary of State for External Affairs saying:
There are, however, three Sikh organizations which exist largely to advocate the creation of an independent Sikh state, known as "Khalistan".
I can understand that there might be organizations that want to promote a separate state, but I do not see that that is necessarily wrong, even within Canada. The letter goes on to
say:
These three organizations are the Babbar Khalsa, the International Sikh Youth Federation and the World Sikh Organization. Some members of these organizations have also engaged in or promote violent activity.
Some members of the Conservative Party have been involved in violent activities. Some members of the New Democratic Party have been involved in violent activities, and even some members of the Liberal Party have been involved in violent activities. Does that mean we tarnish all these organizations as being violent? The letter goes on to say:
The activities of these organizations have been a significant irritant in our relations with India.
I can appreciate they might be an irritant in our relations with India. Some of the activities of the Ukrainian organizations are irritants in our relations with Russia, but that does not mean that we feel that we have any right or obligation to boycott those organizations. Some of the activities of some of the solidarity groups, solidarity groups from Central America, are significant irritants in our relations with the United States. The letter goes on:
The government of India has taken particular exception when elected officials attend functions sponsored by these organizations.
I can understand that the Government of India might take exception. So what, Mr. Speaker? Are we not an independent nation? Are not our elected officials elected to be responsible to the Canadian people? We are not talking about getting involved in subversion in India. We are talking about elected officials meeting with legitimate Canadian organizations. The letter continues:
I would appreciate your co-operation in avoiding events and activities which could be perceived as supporting the Sikh organizations mentioned above or their objective in the creation of an independent Sikh society.
"Activities which could be perceived", and the question is perceived by whom? Perceived by the Indian Government?
March 10, 1988

Obviously the Indian Government is supersensitive on this whole issue.
Reference was made earlier by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), to the establishment of a chair of Sikh studies at the University of British Columbia. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) encouraged the Government to fund the chair. Out of sensitivity to what the Indian Government might perceive as support for the Sikhs, the Department of External Affairs dragged its feet all the way and put up roadblocks against the creation of a chair of Sikh studies at UBC.
A Globe and Mail article for December 13, 1986 points out:
Documents obtained under the Access to Information Act reveal that an External Affairs official believed a federal grant for a chair in Punjabi literature and Sikh studies at the University of British Columbia would be misunderstood by the Government of India.
"While I fully understand that Canada's multiculturalism policies will be guided primarily by Canadian domestic considerations, the implications in terms of foreign policy must also be considered, "E. G. Drake, an Assistant Deputy Minister in External Affairs, wrote in April, 1985 to a Secretary of State official.
Multiculturalism here is being subject to foreign policy considerations. Mr. Drake continued:
"I hope, therefore, that the Indian Government's likely reaction can be taken into account before any conclusion is reached", "he stated.
Mr. Drake wrote that, should federal financing materialize it "would likely be misunderstood by the Government of India and might well cause damage to our bilateral relations with India."
A few weeks ago, when she was resigning, a former assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs referred to the Department of External Affairs as a hotbed of cold feet. I cannot think of a better characterization for this Department. A hotbed of cold feet, and so afraid of our relationship with India that it attempts to subvert our multiculturalism policy.

We see the same kind of cold feet in regard to standing up to France on the St. Pierre-Miquelon issue. We see it in regard to the United States on our Central American policy. We are just not prepared to stand up as a nation. We are so concerned about our bilateral relations with India that we are not prepared to fund a chair of Sikh studies at one of our Canadian universities, which is fully in accordance with Canadian multiculturalism policies.
I was glad to see that the Secretary of State for External Affairs finally went over External Affairs on that issue and a year ago in February there was a grant for the funding of the chair at UBC. Credit has to go not only to the Sikh community, which pushed and advocated the chair but also to my colleague, the New Democratic Party critic for multiculturalism, the Member from Thunder Bay-Nipigon.
What we have with this letter is a slight on an entire community, a slight with no proof. Allegations are made of individual violence but no proof was made of that, and from
Supply
that the entire three organizations are placed beyond the pale for provincial politicians. It is a form, as I said earlier, of McCarthyism.
I object to the effect that this letter has had on my constituents, my friends, on the entire Sikh community and on the entire multicultural community in Canada. Who knows what other letters similar to this one might be in effect? It is an insidious sort of thing. The letter was written in secret. We did not even know what the Secretary of State for External Affairs was thinking about.
I fully support the suggestion by my House Leader, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), that the entire matter should be the subject of investigation by a parliamentary committee. The parliamentary committee should have access to whatever proof the Government thinks it has that these organizations are subversive. It should give access to the Sikh community so that it can come before this organization and state its goals and methods and clear itself. This letter has had the effect of maligning not only these organizations but, by implication, the entire community.
Finally, there should be very clear directions given to the Canadian government organizations that deal with Sikhs and with other multicultural communities, to CSIS, to the RCMP, to the Department of Immigration and to Customs to quit hassling and harassing them and to recognize their rights.
I think it would be in the interests of this House and of the parliamentary democracy of Canada and in the interests of the multicultural policy for the Secretary of State for External Affairs to step back a little bit from his involvement in this issue. I know that he has a personal emotional investment, having written the letter and having had to defend it. If he could step back a little bit and look at the implications of the letter, what it means for the Sikh community, and perhaps get a bit of perspective on his actions, then I think he would want to apologize through the House to the Sikh community.
I believe that the Secretary of State for External Affairs is a person who basically seeks what is best for the Canadian community. I do not think that this letter is worthy of the Secretary of State for External Affairs when he is at his best. I would hope that he would step back, look at the situation, recognize that he made a mistake and apologize to the Canadian people and in particular to the Sikh community.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion we are discussing today is a serious motion. I give the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) credit for the seriousness of his intent. The motion contains within it several items with which I propose to deal separately.
The first paragraph of the motion contains the assertion that the letter in question urges a political boycott of the Sikh

March 10, 1988
Supply
organizations, and there is a further implication later on that Sikhs in general are being affected by this. I would like to remind the Hon. Member that, as he acknowledged earlier in today's debate, I intervened directly on this issue in the House and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) indeed confirmed that it was not his intention in any way, shape or form to inhibit Members of Parliament from meeting with members of these organizations, from listening to their concerns or from becoming informed as to their views or concerns either about the situation in Canada or the situation abroad.
The second paragraph of the motion indicates that this is designed to prevent free and peaceful expressions of the opinions and concerns of Canadians of all origins about events and issues in Canada and in other lands. I am sure the Hon. Member is well aware that there is no prohibition at all on members of these communities meeting with the press, with the media, with Members of Parliament, with provincial Members of Parliament or with Premiers. Nor is there any ban on public meetings or on expressing views very forcefully, nor has there been censorship by the media. Indeed, members of the World Sikh Organization have been able not only to meet with MPs regularly but they have been able to meet with officials of the Department of External Affairs to brief the Department briefly on their particular concerns.
The letter issued by Mr. Clark deals with one specific issue, and that is the issue-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 82-SIKH ORGANIZATIONS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: I must bring to the Hon. Member's attention that it is the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark).

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 82-SIKH ORGANIZATIONS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you have been consistent in your rulings on that all day, and I should have picked it up.
The letter from the Secretary of State for External Affairs deals with the specific issue of attending, on a public platform, a meeting organized by one of the three organizations mentioned and somehow appearing to endorse unwittingly the aims and objectives of the organization. Should there be any doubt as to the aims and objectives of the organization, I would point out that Objective 2.0.2 of the World Sikh Organization is to strive, and I do emphasize, through peaceful means, for the establishment of a Sikh nation, Khalistan, in order to protect the Sikh identity and faith as ordained by the Guru Panth in the daily prayer "Raj Karega Khalsa". The organization clearly calls for the establishment of a separate state in India and in fact for the dismemberment of the country of India. I merely point this out because we in Canada ourselves took offence in 1967 when another foreign power appeared to endorse the aims of groups within our own country which sought the separation of Canada.
I also want to raise another general issue and that is that the United Nations has established codes of conduct for relationships between friendly Governments and for co-operation. One of the principles established by the United Nations in the
twenty-fifth Assembly was that states should refrain from actions aimed at the political independence or the territorial integrity of any state.
We as Canadians were very conscious of outside endorsement of actions which might represent a threat to our territorial integrity. Indeed, because of the general principles established by the United Nations, principles to which we subscribe, we must also be very conscious of appearing to endorse an action which threatens the territorial integrity of another friendly member of the United Nations.
I did mention that while an objective of the World Sikh Organization is to strive to establish Khalistan, it is striving to do this through peaceful means. However, my understanding is that senior members of the organizations, and as the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) indicated, not just ordinary parishioners in the Catholic Church, made emotional statements following Operation Blue Star in 1984, statements which indeed advocated violent activities. To the best of my knowledge, these statements have never been repudiated. This information has been communicated to the organization involved, and certainly I would encourage it to repudiate these alleged statements because they certainly do not conform with my understanding of the group's aims and objectives at this time.
I wish to devote the remainder of my discussion to the assertion which is at the bottom of the first paragraph of the motion which is, that the letter constitutes a demonstration that the Government is undermining the multicultural fabric of Canadian society. In the four years since this Government took office, it has demonstrated time and time again its fervent belief in the concept of multiculturalism. It has done so because it has a deep-rooted belief in human rights and in the equality of all people.
Racism and discrimination have no place in Canada and, in numerous ways, the federal Government has sought to combat and root out manifestations of intolerance and social injustice. While the task is not yet done, we can take pride in what we have accomplished so far. When I say we, I refer not only to the Government but also to all Canadians from coast to coast who are working hard as the Hon. Member for York West who presented the motion today is working hard to make this a land of civility, generosity and openness.
No Government can achieve tolerance and racial harmony by ignoring the situation of its own agencies and Departments. For this reason, the Government has worked hard to see that the multicultural nature of Canada is reflected in the make-up of the federal Public Service. As Members may know, the percentage of our appointments to boards, agencies and commissions from the ethnocultural communities is something like 50 per cent higher than that of the previous Government. At Treasury Board numerous initiatives have been developed to promote employment opportunities for visible minorities. Indeed, the Government introduced an affirmative action program for visible minorities, including the setting of
March 10, 1988

numerical targets. The Public Service Commission is in the process of establishing a network of visible minority coordinators responsible for recruitment, inventory maintenance, marketing and counselling of visible minority candidates. These and other initiatives represent an important start in correcting the imbalance which has long existed in the federal Public Service.
The Government also brought in employment equity legislation in 1986. Under the legislation, Crown corporations and federally-regulated employers with more than 100 employees will be required to provide equitable employment opportunities for designated groups such as women, persons with disabilities, aboriginal peoples, and members of visible minorities. Recently this House gave first reading to Bill C-93, Canada's first multiculturalism Bill. Soon it will receive second reading. When passed, the legislation will affirm a central feature of Canadian life. It will reflect our national conviction that regardless of origin, every Canadian citizen has an equal chance to participate in and contribute to the social, economic, political and cultural life of the country.
Because the Government of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is committed to fairness, it brought in a multiculturalism Bill. Because it stands for equality of opportunity, it brought in an employment equity Bill. Because it clearly appreciates the multicultural reality of Canada, it brought in special measures to promote the employment of visible minorities in federal structures. Therefore, let no Member of the House attempt to mislead Canadians about our Government's commitment to a multiculturalism policy. Let no one attempt to deny our commitment to racial harmony and social equality. Let no one accuse us of attacking anyone's rights, for we sought to do precisely the reverse and safeguard and enhance the rights and opportunities of Canadians.
The concern this Government has shown for minority communities encompasses all groups, religions and ethnic backgrounds. The Sikh community in Canada, like other communities which make up our national fabric, has received financial support for its worthy undertakings in recognition of the contribution it has made to Canadian society. Sikhs have been part of our multicultural nation for many years. They began emigrating to this country at the very beginning of this century. Since then their numbers have grown steadily and they have established roots all across the country. Today Sikh Canadians represent nearly 200,000 Canadians in all provinces, with particularly strong representation in British Columbia and Ontario. With their strong sense of family and their religious belief in morality, selflessness and responsibility, Sikhs have made a contribution to Canadian society greater than their numbers would indicate. They have shown a strong sense of entrepreneurship and made a very real impact on business and in the professions.
Sikhs have integrated well into Canadian society. They have also been diligent in passing on their linguistic and cultural
Supply
heritage from generation to generation. For example, virtually all second generation Sikh Canadians can understand Punjabi. Despite their record of achievement and their exemplary citizenship, Canadian Sikhs, like other visible minorities, are from time to time faced with problems of discrimination, ignorance or prejudice. I personally have been involved in some of these issues for over 10 years, beginning with some of the hard hat cases when I first became an MP 10 year ago, to establishing an immigration policy for Sikh priests and others because their religious needs were not being adequately recognized by the Government.
Equality of opportunity in the workplace and in society generally is of major concern. Sikhs are naturally concerned by the reporting of events in the Punjab and by what they feel is often a stereotyped depiction of their people, one which tends to overlook the very real contribution they have made to Canadian society. Indeed, I can cite a personal example of this in my own riding where the Sikh community is in the process of attempting to construct a new church. The reaction from the community was, my gosh, these are violent people, they must not build this anywhere close to our neighbourhood. Indeed, I took the opportunity to testify in Scarborough Council of my personal knowledge of the congregation and their belief in peace and their positive contribution to society.
In working to combat prejudice and discrimination, Canada's Sikh community, like other minority groups, received a good deal of direct and indirect support from the Canadian Government. The federal Government, through the Secretary of State's multicultural program, provided and continues to provide strong support to Canadian Sikhs. During the past two fiscal years, for example, more than $500,000 in grant money has been provided for some 64 individual projects. Many of those grants have gone toward school and educational projects to help new generations of Sikh Canadians understand and appreciate their heritage and retain and reinforce their traditional language skills. Others have gone to support cultural activities and programs aimed at better educating and informing other Canadians about Sikh Canadians.
One particularly important step was the Secretary of State's agreement to provide major financing support for the establishment of the chair in Punjabi language, literature and Sikh studies at the University of B.C. This chair, established last fall, received a $350,000 federal grant covering 50 per cent of the total required funding. Establishment of this chair represents the culmination of some four years of discussions and co-operative planning in which I was deeply involved, involving the Federation of Sikh Societies in Canada, the University of British Columbia, and the Department of the Secretary of State. Its goal is to initiate and promote research, both at the graduate and at the undergraduate level, in the areas of Punjabi language and literature as well as Sikhism, Sikh history and other aspects of Sikh studies.
The chair has established a focal point for generating a better understanding of Canada's pluralistic and multicultural

March 10, 1988
Supply
nature, and of Sikhs and Sikhism in Canada. It will conduct research into the contributions Sikhs have made to Canadian society and will encourage publication of this research so Canadians will have a better understanding and appreciation of this contribution. All in all, this new chair will make a valuable contribution to our knowledge and understanding, and I am proud our Government has played such a major role in its development and to have been involved so personally in seeing it established.
I might also mention that our Government provided major funding for a conference of Sikhism at the University of Toronto just over a year ago. This Government has given more support and encouragement to Canada's diverse ethnic communities than any other in our history. I think the Secretary of State summed it up well when he said a multicultural Canada is an enriched Canada. The more successfully we share our different cultural backgrounds, the more harmonious and unified we become as a society. The Sikh community, he said, has contributed much to our society. They have strived to meet the complexity and challenges of integration into the mainstream of Canadian life while still retaining the essential qualities of their own unique heritage.
Hard-working Sikh people have contributed much to Canada's economic prosperity and cultural richness. This Government will continue to work with vigour with all our culture minorities, as we have over the past three and a half years. We will help them retain their distinctive qualities, their cultural and language. We will also help them to integrate and achieve full participation in Canadian society. We will work with them to combat prejudice and ignorance wherever they exist in society. This is a commitment we have lived up to in the past and we have reaffirmed that commitment in the multiculturalism Bill which this House will be considering next week.
In summary, I do not think that when one examines the actions of the Government one can conceivably sustain the assertion in the first paragraph of the resolution that this Government has been undermining the multicultural fabric of Canadian society.

Mr. Speaker, I will try not to repeat the mistake. The Member asks whether I think it would be appropriate to establish a special committee. I think it may be, but not as a first step. I met for over three hours yesterday with representatives of Sikh organizations. There are two issues that have been raised.
First, the community has a feeling that it is being harassed by statements in the press or, indeed, by activities of CSIS. I told the members that, with regard to the activities of CSIS Parliament made a decision when it established CSIS that, unlike in the United States where the CIA and the FBI are subject to congressional oversight, a different mechanism would be set up in Canada with regard to CSIS. That mechanism was to provide a special committee of former Members of the House, Privy Councillors all, of different Parties under the chairmanship of the Hon. Ron Atkey, a former distinguished Member of this House. I suggested that an appropriate first step for the organizations involved would be to approach the CSIS oversight committee and take up their allegations with it, which is not directly in Parliament.
With regard to the other issues as to whether there were or were not statements made which advocated violence, which certainly run contrary to the constitution of the World Sikh Organization in Canada, those allegations were brought to the attention of members of the organization yesterday. I am sure that they will want to take the time to examine whether the statements were made by senior members of their organization. If so, since they run contrary to the constitution of the organization, they may feel that it is an opportune time to state categorically that these do not represent the aims and objectives of the organization in order that the WSO would not be seen to be in a position of advocating violence even though in the past, in a very emotional moment, individual senior officers might well have made statements which have that direct interpretation.
Finally, if the organizations involved cannot achieve resolution of their problems through the first two steps which I think should be taken, I would indeed be willing to meet with them again to discuss the possibility of further pursuing the issue in one of the standing committees.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 82-SIKH ORGANIZATIONS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not take part in this debate with any great satisfaction in being able to criticize the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). I regard him as a decent man with great respect for people and I am sorry to see him embroiled in this kind of a controversy. I cannot imagine why he signed the letter that
March 10, 1988

went to the provinces. I would normally have expected him to be very much more sensitive.
The Hon. Member for York Scarborough (Mr. McCrossan) who has just spoken made reference to how Canadians felt when a French visitor seemed to be encouraging separatism. Perhaps it is reasonable for the Secretary of State for External Affairs to tell provincial Premiers what his views are on certain sensitivities and how he would like them treated. However, unfortunately the form of this particular letter was such that it caused a great deal of pain to Canadian citizens.
What was wrong with the letter? For one thing it pointed to three Sikh organizations. However, organizations do not commit terrorist activities or cause difficulties for the host country; individuals do. The World Sikh Organization has some 20,000 members. The International Sikh Youth Federation is only two years old and has perhaps 2,000 members, and Babbar Khalsa has perhaps 200 members. Therefore, a very large and established organization was included, perhaps inappropriately, with two other organizations. In any case, to talk about organizations as if they were all-embracing, as if every individual who belongs to an organization shares the same views, surely is not realistic, as has been pointed out several times today.
The pain which was caused to Canadians of Sikh origin by the release of this letter added to the pain which they have been suffering ever since the Air India disaster. Many people have forgotten that terrorists do not spare their own. There were Sikhs who died in the Air India disaster too.
I was privileged to attend a religious service last July which was sponsored by many groups including the Vishnu Temple, the Kannada Sangha, the Hindu Sabha Mandir, the Bharati Kala Manram, the Hindu Prarthana Samaj, the Hindu Federation, the Zorastrian Society of Ontario, and the Association of Women of India in Canada. It was a memorial service for the victims of the Air India disaster, a most moving expression where prayers were offered by, among others, Sikhs. Prayers were also offered by Christians, Islamics, Hindus, Jainists, Buddhists, and people from the Jewish and Zorastrian faiths. It was a most poignant expression of grief for the deaths of many people but it was grief without bitterness. As one person who lost his two sons said:
The fact we are all victims here together sharing our grief makes life
liveable.
That is the kind of spirit that I have seen in the Sikhs whom I have come to know well since that Air India disaster. Sikhs in Canada are, for the most part, peaceful people. They have been horrified by the terrorism from which they too have suffered. They do not condone it. They have been pained by the assumption that they accept terrorism.
I have here a statement of the objectives of the World Sikh Organization. The first is to promote and follow the teachings of the ten gurus. The second is to strive through peaceful means for the establishment of a Sikh nation, Khalistan, in order to protect the Sikh identity. The fourth is to work for the
Supply
promotion of ideals of universal brotherhood, peace, justice, freedom of worship and speech, respect for cultural diversity and human dignity for all, without any distinction as per the instruments and covenants of the United Nations Organization.
These are very worthy objectives. As has been said, in an organization of 20,000, one cannot guarantee that every individual subscribes to those objectives. However, those are the objectives of the organization.
The organization has taken some steps over the years to dissociate itself from violence. I have a copy of a letter dated May 14, 1985, from the General Secretary of the World Sikh Organization to the National Councils of the U.S.A., Canada and the United Kingdom. It reads:
WSO constitution lays down that we are a peaceful organization working for human rights of Sikhs in India. Therefore, Membership Screening Committee in your countries should be instructed not to accept membership from known or proved terrorists and any member who is guilty of terrorism should be removed from WSO membership according to our constitution.
Another letter dated April 2, 1985, from the General Secretary to the National Councils of Canada, the United States and the United Kingdom reads in part: "We would appeal that the utmost care should be taken to avoid violence and provocation. Meetings and processions should be strictly in accordance with the laws of the land". It goes on: "We must fully co-operate with the authorities and abide by the laws of the land". Those are the stated purposes of the World Sikh Organization.
We are all aware of the violence in the Punjab. I was there a year ago and the situation indeed is one where grievances over riparian rights and religious differences have escalated over the years. They are not being solved by political or democratic means. There is violence on the part of Sikh terrorists and there is violence on the part of others. It is a country where the habeas corpus does not operate and people are detained without trial for very long periods. There are allegations of torture and mistreatment.
Surely citizens of Canada are entitled to talk to their Members of Parliament and provincial politicians about their concerns for the human rights of their relatives and friends in another country.
This has been the case with people in a long list of countries. There are many organizations here which exist to keep us aware of conditions in their country of origin. We have always claimed that this is part of their democratic rights.
Of course, none of us wants to encourage violence. None of us will have much time for anybody who is acting in any way against the laws of our land. However, I suggest that Canadians of Sikh origin by and large are excellent citizens. They are thrifty, hard working, peaceful people who are very family oriented. It has been a source of great pain to them that there

March 10, 1988
Adjournment Debate
is so much violence in their own country of origin and that some of that violence has shown in Canada.
The statements I have read make it clear that the World Sikh Organization does not condone violence. I think it behooves all of us to ensure that Canadians are able to exercise their democratic rights and express their concerns about conditions in their country of origin as long as they do it in peaceful ways. Whole communities should not be tarred with the excesses of a few, the excesses which the communities themselves have condemned and made clear they do not support.
